self: You, an Athenian, as your fellow citizens resolve to abandon the city and fight on the sea for Greece's freedom, propose they stay at home and open the gates to the Persian king, thinking it expedient.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: a man named Cyrsilus proposed that they should stay at home and open the gates of their city to Xerxes
source_reason: he was working for what he thought was expediency
source_lesson: And yet he was working for what he thought was expediency; but it was not — not at all, for it clashed with moral rectitude.
source_verdict: And yet he was working for what he thought was expediency; but it was not — not at all, for it clashed with moral rectitude.
stoic_judgement: He treats keeping the city, homes and lives (things not up to us) as the good to secure, even at the price of submitting to the Persian king and abandoning Greece's freedom. The words that show this: "propose they stay at home and open the gates to the Persian king, thinking it expedient."
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a bad judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8): craving the externals of safety and property, which ends 'by subordinating himself to others' who can grant or take them (Discourses 1.4). Even if he sincerely holds it expedient, a wrong view harms the one deceived (Handbook 42). In his role as citizen (R6, Discourses 2.10), proposing to give up his country's freedom is to 'disregard the interests of one's country' (DL 7.108).

contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.60)
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, giving historical examples in his treatise of moral advice (addressed to his son)
source_quote: would debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of their city and would exclude them from its borders
source_lesson: Still, to debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of the city is altogether contrary to the laws of humanity.
source_verdict: They, too, do wrong who would debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of their city and would exclude them from its borders
stoic_judgement: Most likely he treats the city's advantages as goods owed to citizens alone, and foreigners as outsiders with no claim on what is due between people. The scene says he will 'debar foreigners from enjoying the advantages of the city and exclude them from its borders'. This is a blanket exclusion of a whole class, and no emergency, law or other reason is given. A less likely reading is that he acts from his office, guarding the city's interest as a magistrate should.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R8, a wholesale refusal of what is shared to people because they are foreign most likely proceeds from a wrong judgement about what is due to others, which is a failure of justice (kindness, good fellowship, fair dealing). By R6, a magistrate's role does ask him to care for his city (DL 7.108), so acting from a correct judgement in that role keeps real weight.

source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, addressing his son Cicero (the addressee of the book)
source_quote: when he decided that it was more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another, he slew his brother. He threw to the winds his brotherly affection and his human feelings, to secure what seemed to him — but was not — expedient
source_reason: it was the specious appearance of expediency that actuated him; and when he decided that it was more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another

source_verdict: He committed a crime, therefore, with due respect to him let me say so, be he Quirinus or Romulus.
stoic_judgement: He treats sole rule (an office, something not up to him) as a good worth more than his brother's life and his own good faith. The words that show it: "because he has decided that it is more expedient for him to reign alone than to share the throne with another."
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from the bad judgement that an external (office, power) is good, so it is badly done (R1, R2; Handbook 1, 19; Discourses 1.29). It also violates what his role as brother asks (R6; Handbook 30; Diogenes Laertius 7.108: to neglect one's brothers is contrary to duty).

other: You see a wise man who is starving to death take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society, merely for his own benefit.
self: You are a wise man starving to death, and you take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society, merely for your own benefit.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, answering a question he puts in the mouth of a hypothetical objector ('someone may say')
source_quote: suppose a wise man were starving to death, might he not take the bread of some perfectly useless member of society?
source_reason: merely for one's own benefit
source_lesson: We are not to say, therefore, that sickness or want or any evil of that sort is more repugnant to Nature than to covet and to appropriate what is one's neighbour's; but we do maintain that disregard of the common interests is repugnant to Nature; for it is unjust.
source_verdict: Not at all; for my life is not more precious to me than that temper of soul which would keep me from doing wrong to anybody for my own advantage. ... For, if merely for one's own benefit one were to take something away from a man, though he were a perfectly worthless fellow, it would be an act of meanness and contrary to Nature's law. But suppose one would be able, by remaining alive, to render signal service to the state and to human society — if from that motive one should take something from another, it would not be a matter for censure. ... And therefore Nature's law itself, which protects and conserves human interests, will surely determine that a man who is wise, good, and brave, should in emergency have the necessaries of life transferred to him from a person who is idle and worthless; for the good man's death would be a heavy loss to the common weal; only let him beware that self-esteem and self-love do not find in such a transfer of possessions a pretext for wrong-doing.
stoic_judgement: He treats his own survival, his body, which is not up to him, as a good great enough to justify taking what is another's. He also seems to treat the other's 'uselessness' as cancelling that person's claim to his own bread. The words 'merely for his own benefit' show that he acts for his body, not for any duty to others, and 'perfectly useless member of society' suggests the excuse he leans on.
stoic_reason: Under R1, R2 and R6, the essence of evil is a certain kind of moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). Here the body and the bread are externals that he values above being just and faithful toward another member of society, so he acts badly. Life is a preferred indifferent, but taking another's due for oneself is contrary to correct reason, and the scene gives no motive beyond his own benefit.

other: You see the Athenians in Assembly reject unheard a secret plan to burn the Spartan fleet, reported as highly expedient but not morally right, concluding what is not morally right is not expedient.
self: You, sitting in the Athenian Assembly, reject unheard a secret plan to burn the Spartan fleet, reported as highly expedient but not morally right, concluding what is not morally right is not expedient.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, addressing his son Marcus
source_quote: at the instance of Aristides they rejected the whole proposition without even listening to it
source_reason: the Athenians concluded that what was not morally right was likewise not expedient
source_lesson: Let it be set down as an established principle, then, that what is morally wrong can never be expedient — not even when one secures by means of it that which one thinks expedient; for the mere act of thinking a course expedient, when it is morally wrong, is demoralizing.
source_verdict: Their attitude was better than ours; for we let pirates go scot free, while we make our allies pay tribute.
stoic_judgement: The Athenians treat moral rightness as the measure of advantage. A gain such as destroying the Spartan fleet is no good to them if it must be won by a wrong act. The vignette shows this in 'reject unheard a secret plan ... reported as highly expedient but not morally right, concluding what is not morally right is not expedient.'
stoic_reason: The act comes from a correct judgement: the good lies in moral purpose, and externals like naval power are only materials for it (Discourses 1.29). They refuse an advantage that requires a wrong act toward neighbours, so they act well (R1, R5). The deed is a refusal of injustice and secret harm, so it falls under justice (R8).

source_quote: the one who had been condemned to death requested a few days’ respite for the purpose of putting his loved ones in the care of friends, the other became surety for his appearance, with the understanding that his friend did not return, he himself should be put to death. And when the friend returned on the day appointed
source_reason: for the purpose of putting his loved ones in the care of friends
source_lesson: Well then, when we are weighing what seems to be expedient in friendship against what is morally right, let apparent expediency be disregarded and moral rectitude prevail; and when in friendship requests are submitted that are not morally right, let conscience and scrupulous regard for the right take precedence of the obligations of friendship.
source_verdict: enjoyed such ideally perfect friendship ... in admiration for their faithfulness
stoic_judgement: He treats keeping faith with his friend, and letting the friend do his duty to his loved ones, as worth more than his own life, and treats his death as not an evil to be avoided at the cost of fidelity. The scene shows this in 'become surety for his friend, condemned to death by the tyrant', 'to put his loved ones in the care of friends', and 'if his friend does not return, he himself will be put to death'.
stoic_reason: His life and body are not up to him and are materials for moral purpose (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). Death is nothing dreadful (Handbook 5). The most likely judgement behind the pledge is that being faithful to a friend is the good, so the act proceeds from correct judgement and is well done in the role of friend (R1, R6). A first movement or an indifferent act-type (R7) has no support here, and neither does a vain motive (R1: do not invent one).

self: You, a statesman kept by armed treason from politics and the bar, turn your forced leisure and solitude to account, having learned that among evils one should extract any good they contain.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
chapter: The Conflict between the Right and the Expedient
speaker: Cicero, writing to his son Marcus
source_quote: I am turning my leisure to account — though it is not such repose as the man should be entitled to who once brought the state repose from civil strife — and I am not letting this solitude, which necessity and not my will imposes on me, find me idle.
source_reason: But I have learned from philosophers that among evils one ought not only to choose the least, but also to extract even from these any element of good that they may contain.
source_lesson: But I have learned from philosophers that among evils one ought not only to choose the least, but also to extract even from these any element of good that they may contain.
source_verdict: But I have learned from philosophers that among evils one ought not only to choose the least, but also to extract even from these any element of good that they may contain. For that reason, I am turning my leisure to account
stoic_judgement: He treats his exclusion from office as outside his control and his use of it as up to him. 'turning his forced leisure and solitude to account' shows he takes the loss of politics and the bar as material for his moral purpose, not as a ruin. 'among evils' hints that he may still count the exclusion an evil.
stoic_reason: Office and reputation are not under our control (Handbook 1). Externals are 'materials for the moral purpose' (Discourses 1.29), and he makes correct use of them, as a man making progress does (R1, R5). Some weight goes to 'badly', because calling a rejected indifferent an 'evil' may be a faulty judgement (R2). But the act he chooses proceeds from a sound judgement.

self: You know your house is unsanitary, vermin-ridden and built of unsound timber, and you keep these facts from the purchaser for your own profit, selling it for far more than it is worth.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, posing the case and deciding between the arguments of Antipater and Diogenes
source_quote: the vendor does not tell the purchaser these facts but sells him the house for far more than he could reasonably have expected to get for it
source_reason: trying for your own profit to keep others from finding out something that you know, when it is for their interest to know it
source_lesson: I think, then, that it was the duty of that grain-dealer not to keep back the facts from the Rhodians, and of this vendor of the house to deal in the same way with his purchaser.
source_verdict: And who fails to discern what manner of concealment that is and what sort of person would be guilty of it? At all events he would be no candid or sincere or straightforward or upright or honest man, but rather one who is shifty, sly, artful, shrewd, underhand, cunning, one grown old in fraud and subtlety.
stoic_judgement: He treats the profit, an external not up to him, as a good worth more than good faith toward the buyer. The vignette shows this in "knows his house is unsanitary, vermin-ridden and built of unsound timber", "keep these facts from the purchaser for his own profit" and "selling it for far more than it is worth".
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from the judgement that gain is good, so it is badly done (R1, Discourses 4.8; Discourses 1.29: externals are only materials for the moral purpose). He knowingly hides serious defects, overcharges, and gives up being faithful for an external (Discourses 1.4; Handbook 52 on deceit). In a seller's role this is contrary to what is due to the other party (R6).

self: You, a shepherd of the king made invisible by turning a gold ring, murder your royal master with the queen's assistance, without anyone's being able to detect you.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, citing Plato
source_quote: And so, with the advantage which the ring gave him, he debauched the queen, and with her assistance he murdered his royal master and removed all those who he thought stood in his way, without anyone’s being able to detect him in his crimes. Thus, by virtue of the ring, he shortly rose to be king of Lydia.
source_lesson: Now, suppose a wise man had just such a ring, he would not imagine that he was free to do wrongly any more than if he did not have it; for good men aim to secure not secrecy but the right.
source_verdict: without anyone’s being able to detect him in his crimes
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats what the murder gains him, his master's place and power, as a good worth killing for. Because he is unseen ('made invisible by turning a gold ring', 'without anyone's being able to detect him'), he also seems to treat being found out, not the wrong itself, as the only thing to avoid. The deliberate, planned killing of 'his royal master' with an accomplice ('with the queen's assistance') shows a considered act, not a reflex.
stoic_reason: A planned murder of the master he serves is an act reason forbids and a breach of what his role owes (Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10). It proceeds from the false judgement that externals not up to him, such as power and safety from detection, are goods, so it is badly done (Discourses 4.8; R1, R6). It is no first movement and no indifferent act (R3, R7).

other: You see a leading Roman citizen, named joint-heir by forgers in a will he suspects is forged, accept the legacy meant for the dead man's nephew, being conscious of no personal guilt.
self: You, a leading Roman citizen named joint-heir by forgers in a will you suspect is forged, accept the legacy meant for the dead man's nephew, being conscious of no personal guilt.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, arguing in his own voice in On Duties Book III
source_quote: Although these men suspected that the will was a forgery, still, as they were conscious of no personal guilt in the matter, they did not spurn the miserable boon procured through the crime of others.
source_reason: as they were conscious of no personal guilt in the matter
source_lesson: For if he does wrong who does not ward off and repel injury when he can — as I explained in the course of the First Book — what is to be thought of the man who not only does not try to prevent wrong, but actually aids and abets it?
source_verdict: Is this excuse competent to acquit them of guilt? I cannot think so, although I loved the one while he lived, and do not hate the other now that he is dead.
stoic_judgement: He treats the inheritance, an external, as a good worth taking. He also treats his own innocence of the forgery as enough to make the taking blameless, even though he believes the money rightly belongs to someone else. The words that show this: 'in a will he suspects is forged, accept the legacy meant for the dead man's nephew, being conscious of no personal guilt.'
stoic_reason: Property is not up to us and is only material for the moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). Knowingly keeping what he suspects is due to another, and excusing it because he did not forge the will himself, proceeds from the bad judgement that gain outweighs fair dealing (R1). It is like being 'ready with the arguments' while still doing wrong (Handbook 52). A leading citizen's role makes this worse, not better (R6).

source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: There before the Roman People he accused his own general, an eminent man and one of our first citizens, of purposely protracting the war
source_reason: declared that if they would make him consul, he would within a short time deliver Jugurtha alive or dead into the hands of the Roman People
source_lesson: But for all cases we have one rule, with which I desire you to be perfectly familiar: that which seems expedient must not be morally wrong; or, if it is morally wrong, it must not seem expedient.
source_verdict: And so he was elected consul, it is true, but he was a traitor to his own good faith and to justice; for by a false charge he subjected to popular disfavour an exemplary and highly respected citizen
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the consulship and the glory of ending the war, which are not up to him, as a good worth winning, even at the cost of truth and of his duty to his general. The vignette shows this: he 'falsely accuse[s]' his own general 'before the Roman People' and pairs the charge with a promise 'if made consul he will soon deliver the enemy king alive or dead'.
stoic_reason: The act comes from a judgement that office and reputation are goods. Epictetus says such a person 'will not wish to be... a consul, but a free man' (Handbook 19), and acting from that craving is acting badly (R1, R2). In his role as lieutenant he owes good faith to his general (R6). Even if he half-believes the charge, a wrong judgement is still his fault (Handbook 42).

self: You asked the vendor of a farm to name his price definitely, and you reply that you consider it worth more and pay him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked.
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero, in his philosophical treatise (later citing Hecaton's contrary opinion of the act)
source_quote: he replied that he considered it worth more, and paid him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked
source_reason: he replied that he considered it worth more
source_lesson: Here, then, is that mischievous idea — the world accounting some men upright, others wise; and it is this fact that gives Ennius occasion to say:
source_verdict: No one could say that this was not the act of an honest man; but people do say that it was not the act of a worldly-wise man, any more than if he had sold for a smaller amount than he could have commanded.
stoic_judgement: He treats fair dealing as more important than gain. Money is an external he will not take at the seller's expense, and he wants to pay what the farm is truly worth: 'reply that he considers it worth more, and pay him 100,000 sesterces over and above what he asked.'
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a judgement that the good lies in his own just choice, not in the external of a cheaper purchase (R1, Discourses 1.29, 4.8). As a buyer (R6), he gives the vendor his due. This is fair dealing under justice, with restraint of the appetite for gain (R8). He acts well as a person making progress (R5). Overpaying from vanity, or careless loss of property, is possible, but the scene gives no hint of either.

other: You see a banker of Syracuse ask the fishermen to do their fishing in front of his villa, then tell a Roman knight seeking a country seat, "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are."
self: You, a banker of Syracuse, ask the fishermen to do their fishing in front of your villa, then tell a Roman knight seeking a country seat, "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are."
source: Cicero, On Duties III (44 BCE; Walter Miller, 1913)
speaker: Cicero
source_quote: When this fact was spread abroad, one Pythius, a banker of Syracuse, informed him that he had such an estate; that it was not for sale, however, but Canius might make himself at home there, if he pleased; and at the same time he invited him to the estate to dinner next day. Canius accepted. Then Pythius, who, as might be expected of a moneylender, could command favours of all classes, called the fishermen together and asked them to do their fishing the next day out in front of his villa, and told them what he wished them to do. ... "No wonder," answered Pythius; "this is where all the fish in Syracuse are; here is where the fresh water comes from; the fishermen cannot get along without this estate." ... Inflamed with desire for it, Canius insisted upon Pythius's selling it to him. At first he demurred. To make a long story short, Canius gained his point. The man was rich, and, in his desire to own the country seat, he paid for it all that Pythius asked; and he bought the entire equipment, too. Pythius entered the amount upon his ledger and completed the transfer.
source_lesson: No act of theirs can be expedient, when what they do is tainted with so many vices.
source_verdict: Pythius, therefore, and all others who do one thing while they pretend another are faithless, dishonest, and unprincipled scoundrels.
source_missing: That no fishermen normally fished there, so the display was staged and the claim was false. Pythius did it to trick Canius, who wanted a country seat, into buying the estate at a high price, while pretending it was not for sale.
stoic_judgement: He treats getting the knight's money, an external not up to him, as a good worth gaining by deceit. The scene shows this: he arranges in advance for the fishermen to fish 'in front of his villa', and then tells a man 'seeking a country seat' the falsehood that 'this is where all the fish in Syracuse are.' The staging and the lie point to a plan to sell the villa at a false value.
stoic_reason: This is active deceit, not mere silence: he stages a false impression and backs it with a lie in order to profit (Handbook 52). It proceeds from the bad judgement that gain is a good, so it is badly done (Discourses 4.8, R1), and it fails what is due to the buyer in good faith and fair dealing (R8).

That fits Handbook 52 on deceit and the Discourses 1.29 point that externals are only materials for the moral purpose, so 'badly' is most likely. By R9, though, Epictetus gives no rule on what a seller must disclose, and silence without a spoken lie is not settled by his framing.

The vignette shows this in 'wish for the death of his son, because he is suspicious of the son's relations with his step-mother': he acts on suspicion, not knowledge.
stoic_reason: He assents rashly to an unverified impression (the third field, Discourses 3.2) and acts from the judgement that an external harm justifies destroying his son. That is a choice proceeding from bad judgement, so it is badly done (Discourses 4.8, R1). It also inverts what his role as a father asks, which is care for his son (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10, R6).

source_verdict: He was wrong; for deceit does not remove the guilt of perjury — it merely aggravates it. His cunning that impudently tried to masquerade as prudence was, therefore, only folly. And so the senate ordered that the cunning scoundrel should be taken back to Hannibal in chains.
stoic_judgement: He treats staying safe and free at Rome, which is not up to him, as a greater good than keeping his sworn word, and he uses a quibble to excuse breaking it. The scene shows this in 'go back on the pretext of forgetting something' and 'explaining that his return released him from his oath'.
stoic_reason: The act comes from a bad judgement (R1, R2): he takes an external (body, place, freedom) for a good and gives up good faith, the part of moral purpose that is truly his own, to get it. Like Handbook 52, he is 'ready with the arguments' while acting deceitfully. His role as one bound by his oath asks him to return (R6).

The pairing of "does not in general agree with ... Antisthenes" with "does not know" hints at the second reading, but does not show it.
stoic_reason: Under the third field (Discourses 3.2), declining to assent rashly to an impression is acting well (R1). If his "I do not know" is a dodge rooted in partisanship, it is a failure of fair dealing and honesty. The scene gives no clear sign of which judgement prompts him (Handbook 45), so no reading is clearly most likely.

stoic_judgement: He treats his father's escape from prosecution (an external, not up to him) as a good he must secure, even by threatening to kill a magistrate. He also treats his duty to his father as binding despite the father's harshness to him. The vignette shows this in 'banished him from all companionship', 'hear his father is in trouble on his account', and 'draw a sword and swear to kill the tribune ... unless he swears to withdraw the suit'.
stoic_reason: His loyalty to a harsh father fits his role as a son (Handbook 30: 'He is a father'). But by Discourses 1.11, affection is right only when it is also reasonable. Coercing an official with a threat of murder is an act reason forbids, so it comes from a bad judgement (R1, R6): the judgement that his father's acquittal, an external, must be had at any price.

He also judges that his role as teacher calls for correcting it. The vignette shows this in "declaring nothing more unbecoming than arrogance" and in the setting: a student who "insisted on joining his class" is seated deliberately "to soil his cloak, then among the beggars."
stoic_reason: Under R1, the act proceeds from a correct judgement: good and evil lie only in moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), and the cloak and wealth are indifferent materials. Under R6, correcting a student's vanity is what the designation of teacher suggests (Discourses 2.10). The small chance of 'badly' allows that he values humbling for its own sake, which the scene does not state.

source_verdict: One day at a banquet he was reclining in silence and was asked the reason: whereupon he bade his critic carry word to the king that there was one present who knew how to hold his tongue.
stoic_judgement: He treats restraint of speech as his own good: his silence and his words "one present who knows how to hold his tongue" show it. He treats the impression he makes on the king, and the talk expected at a banquet, as not his concern.
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a judgement about what is up to him, his own speech (Handbook 1), not from craving the applause or approval of the king, which is not up to him (Discourses 2.13). So by R1 it is well done, and by R8 it shows self-restraint over the impulse to speak. A boastful reading is possible, but the scene gives no sign of vanity.

self: You notice the slave of one of your acquaintances marked with weals and say to the acquaintance, "I see the imprints of your anger."
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)
speaker: Diogenes Laertius, recounting anecdotes about Zeno of Citium
source_quote: Once when he saw the slave of one of his acquaintance marked with weals, "I see," said he, "the imprints of your anger."
source_verdict: "I see," said he, "the imprints of your anger."
stoic_judgement: The philosopher most likely treats the master's anger as the real evil in the scene and judges it right to name it frankly. The words that suggest this: he 'notice[s] the slave ... marked with weals' and tells the master, 'I see the imprints of your anger.' He blames the master's passion, not the slave, and he does it in words, with no anger of his own shown.
stoic_reason: Epictetus traces acts to judgements and holds that anger is a faulty judgement that harms the angry man's own moral purpose (Handbook 5, 20; Discourses 1.18). Pointing this out to the master, out of concern for what is due to the slave and to the master, proceeds from a correct judgement and so is acting well while making progress (R1, R2, R5). The remark gives little hint of vanity or reproach for its own sake, so 'badly' gets only a small probability.

source_verdict: He was renowned for his industry, being indeed driven by extreme poverty to work for a living.
stoic_judgement: He treats the study and practice of philosophy, the care of his own moral purpose, as what matters. He treats his poverty and the hard night labour as externals to be borne and not reasons to give up. Evidence: "driven by extreme poverty to work for a living", "by day exercise himself in arguments", "undertaking this labour for the love of philosophy".
stoic_reason: The vignette states his reason: he endures hardship for the sake of philosophy and does not let poverty, which is not up to him, turn him from what is. This is the man making progress of Discourses 1.4, who keeps his principles in daily practice, so the act proceeds from correct judgement (R1, R5). Enduring hardship and toil falls in the field of courage, with industriousness and perseverance subordinate to it (R8).

self: You are a student of dialectic, and when a dialectician shows you seven logical forms concerned with a sophism and asks a hundred drachmas for them, you promptly pay him two hundred in your love of learning.
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)
speaker: Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Zeno
source_quote: Being told a hundred drachmas, he promptly paid two hundred
source_reason: his love of learning
source_verdict: to such lengths would he go in his love of learning.
stoic_judgement: He treats understanding (training in assent, here how to see through a sophism) as worth far more than money, an external. The vignette shows this in "promptly pay him two hundred in his love of learning": he pays at once, gladly and beyond the asking price.
stoic_reason: By R1 the act is judged by its judgement. Money is only material for the moral purpose (Discourses 1.29), and he gives it freely for training in the third field, the avoidance of error in assent (Discourses 3.2). Paying more than was asked, from goodwill toward the teacher, is a reasonable use of a preferred indifferent, not a craving for externals. He acts well as one making progress (R5). The only reading against this, that he values logic for display or out of order before the first two fields, is not suggested by the scene.

self: You, an old philosopher and head of your school, are finding fault with yourself, and when a fellow philosopher asks, "Who is it you are scolding so?" you laugh and say, "An old man with grey hairs and no wits."
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)
speaker: Diogenes Laertius, narrating the life of Cleanthes
source_quote: He would often find fault with himself too ... he, laughing, said, "An old man with grey hairs and no wits."
source_verdict: Such was he; and yet, although Zeno had many other eminent disciples, he was able to succeed him in the headship of the school.
stoic_judgement: He treats the faults of his own reason as what is truly bad and worth correcting. He does not treat his age, his rank as head of the school, or another's opinion as what matters. This shows in 'finding fault with himself' and in naming the target as 'an old man with grey hairs and no wits.' His laugh suggests the self-rebuke is calm correction, not distress.
stoic_reason: He turns blame on his own moral purpose, the one thing up to him (Discourses 1.29). Epictetus marks this as the beginning of instruction, as opposed to blaming others (Handbook 5). It is also progress: attending to one's own choices while at work, even as an elder and school head (Discourses 1.4, 2.10). The laugh suggests no assented passion of grief or shame (R1, R2 not triggered, R5, R6).

source_verdict: Such was he; and yet, although Zeno had many other eminent disciples, he was able to succeed him in the headship of the school.
stoic_judgement: He treats learning the philosophy, which is the training of his own moral purpose, as worth more than comfort or proper materials. He treats poverty and the lack of paper, which are externals, not as evils that stop him but as materials to work with. The scene suggests this through his writing down his teacher's lectures "on oyster-shells and the blade-bones of oxen, through lack of money to buy paper."
stoic_reason: Poverty and property are not up to him (Handbook 1), and he does not let their lack hinder the study by which progress is made (Discourses 1.4). A careful reader would most likely see an act that proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R5): steady endurance of hardship for the sake of what is his own. Writing notes is in itself an intermediate act, so some weight goes to neither (R7).

stoic_judgement: He treats the insult as no harm to him and not worth anger. He does not count his reputation, which is not up to him, as a good he must defend. The vignette shows this in his acceptance of the apology and in his reasoning: since Dionysus and Heracles were ridiculed by poets without getting angry, 'it would be absurd to be annoyed at casual abuse'.
stoic_reason: It is not the poet who insults him but his own judgement that he is insulted (Handbook 20). He refuses that judgement for a stated reason, so his calm acceptance proceeds from a correct judgement and is acting well (R1, R2, R4). Forgiving the poet is kindness toward a neighbour (R6, R8).

stoic_judgement: He treats the gibes as no harm to him and his own work and study as what matters. The vignette shows this in 'putting up with gibes', 'not minding being called the ass', and his reply that he alone is strong enough to carry his teacher's load, which turns the insult into a statement about his endurance in learning.
stoic_reason: It is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your judgement that he does (Handbook 20). Not minding the name shows he does not assent to the impression that he is wronged, so no passion of anger or shame is assented to (R2), and his calm, witty answer comes from that correct judgement (Discourses 4.8, R1). The words 'he alone' could hint at vanity, a smaller reading.

speaker: Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Cleanthes
source_quote: To some one who declared that Arcesilaus did not do what he ought, his reply was, "No more of this; do not censure him. For if by his words he does away with duty, he maintains it at all events by his deeds."
source_lesson: True, but my flattery consists in alleging that your theory is incompatible with your practice.
source_verdict: No more of this; do not censure him. For if by his words he does away with duty, he maintains it at all events by his deeds.
stoic_judgement: He treats a rival's conduct, not his rival's doctrine, as what deserves praise or blame. He holds that it is unfair to censure a man whose deeds keep to what is appropriate, even if his theory denies it. The words that show this: "do not censure him ... if by his words he does away with duty, he maintains it at all events by his deeds."
stoic_reason: He refuses to join in hasty blame and judges the man by his acts rather than his school's arguments (Handbook 45, Discourses 4.8, R1). Defending a rival from unfair censure is fair dealing and kindness to one's neighbour, so it is an appropriate act done from a correct judgement (R5, R8 justice).

He keeps to what is by nature more fit to be chosen, health and use of his faculties, without craving it (Discourses 2.10). So he acts from correct judgements (Discourses 4.8, R1). His calm, good-humoured reply shows no assented passion (R2).

stoic_judgement: He treats the duties of his role, set by the god, as what he must attend to each day, and arranges a daily reminder of them: he has an attendant say at dawn, "Arise, O king, and attend to the matters that the great Ahuramazda wants you to attend to." Keeping that before him every morning resembles the man in Discourses 1.4 who 'when he rises in the morning proceeds to keep and observe' his principles, so it reads as acting well (R1, R5). The stated belief that all are his slaves is a wrong judgement about what is due to others and pulls toward acting badly (R2, R8 justice), but the scene does not show that belief prompting this act.

source_verdict: As a man, Epictetus replied, and a man who had been proclaimed among the athletes at the Olympic games and had contended in them, a man who had been familiar with such a place, and not merely anointed in Baton's school.
source_missing: The vignette omits that the athlete had been proclaimed a victor at the Olympic games and had really competed there, not merely trained in Baton's school. Epictetus grounds the refusal in that sense of his own character and worth.
stoic_judgement: He most likely judges that death is not an evil, and that losing his manhood would be worse than dying for the person he is ('persist in his resolution', 'a philosopher'). Another reading is possible: he values his body and his athletic identity, both externals, above life ('return to the gymnasium').
stoic_reason: The verdict follows the judgement behind the act (R1). If he holds firm because death is not dreadful (Handbook 5) and because the role he has chosen asks it (Discourses 2.10, R6), he acts well. If he clings to his body or his standing as an athlete as a good, he acts from a judgement about externals (Handbook 1, R2), and refusing life, the preferred indifferent, would be an error. The scene does not make either reading clearly the more likely, so the row is contested.

source_verdict: For he who has once brought himself to deliberate about such matters, and to calculate the value of external things, comes very near to those who have forgotten their own character.
stoic_judgement: He treats his own character, being the one who keeps a noble's self-respect, as the good, and the loss of his head as no evil next to it. The words that show this: he will 'refuse even to deliberate about performing in Nero's spectacles, though refusing may cost his head, because he wishes to be purple, the bright thread that makes the tunic beautiful.'
stoic_reason: His stated reason places the good in his moral purpose and his chosen role (Discourses 1.29, 2.10; R1, R6). He treats life, office and safety as externals not up to him (Handbook 1), so he acts from a correct judgement and acts well (Discourses 4.8; R5). A smaller chance remains that 'wishes to be purple' reads as a wish for distinction in others' eyes, which would be an external.

self: You, blamed by your teacher for not having discovered the one thing omitted in a certain syllogism, reply, "I suppose that I have burnt the Capitol."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.7.32–33 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: Of the use of sophistical arguments and hypothetical and the like.
speaker: Epictetus, recounting how his teacher Musonius Rufus rebuked him when, as a student, he missed the flaw in a syllogism
source_quote: not having discovered the one thing omitted in a certain syllogism: I suppose, I said, that I have burnt the Capitol.
source_lesson: But for a man to use the appearances presented to him rashly and foolishly and carelessly, and not to understand argument, nor demonstration, nor sophism, nor, in a word, to see in questioning and answering what is consistent with that which we have granted or is not consistent; is there no error in this?
source_verdict: But for a man to use the appearances presented to him rashly and foolishly and carelessly, and not to understand argument, nor demonstration, nor sophism, nor, in a word, to see in questioning and answering what is consistent with that which we have granted or is not consistent; is there no error in this?
stoic_judgement: He treats his error in reasoning as a trifle that does not merit blame, nothing like a real wrong. The words that show this: 'I suppose that I have burnt the Capitol', a retort that sets his slip against a great crime to make it look small.
stoic_reason: For Epictetus the power to make correct use of impressions is 'the most excellent faculty', and carelessness in assent is the third field of training (Discourses 1.1, 3.2). To judge a fault in one's own reasoning a small thing, and to brush off the correction a student's role calls for, is a bad judgement about what is good and bad (R1, R6).
also_in: Musonius Rufus, Lectures / Fragments (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)

self: You leave home when your little daughter is sick and supposed to be in danger, because you cannot endure to stay with her, till a person sends news she has recovered.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.11.1–4,20–26 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a visiting magistrate
source_quote: lately, when my little daughter was sick and was supposed to be in danger, I could not endure to stay with her, but I left home till a person sent me news that she had recovered.
source_reason: I acted naturally, the man replied. ... This is the case, said the man, with all or at least most fathers.
source_lesson: And in a word, neither death nor exile nor pain nor anything of the kind is the cause of our doing anything or not doing; but our own opinions and our wills \(δόγματα\).
source_verdict: Well then to leave your sick child and to go away is not reasonable, and I suppose that you will not say that it is ... But if this is so, it results that your behaviour was not at all an affec- tionate act.
stoic_judgement: He treats his daughter's illness and possible death, which are not up to him, as an evil too dreadful to watch, and he puts his own relief from that distress ahead of what he owes her as her father. The words that show this: "leave home, because he cannot endure to stay with her" while she "is sick and supposed to be in danger".
stoic_reason: His flight comes from an assented passion: the judgement that something outside his control is a terrible evil (Handbook 5; Discourses 2.13; R2). It is not a passing first movement (R3), since he acts on it and stays away until the news comes. His affection is not the fault, but here it is not joined with reason (Discourses 1.11), and it leads him to neglect what his role as a father asks: to stay and care for his sick child (Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10; DL 7.108; R6).

source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.9.27–28 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How from the fact that we are akin to God a man may proceed to the consequences.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting an episode from his own experience
source_quote: when he had read the letter, he gave it back to me and said, "I wished for your help, not your pity: no evil has happened to me."
source_reason: no evil has happened to me
source_lesson: But if he were anything more, lie would know that one man is not miserable through the means of another.
source_verdict: But when a man is cowardly and mean, what else must be done for him than to write letters as you would about a corpse.
stoic_judgement: He treats the loss of wealth and rank as no evil ("no evil has happened to me"). He treats pity, and a letter that grovels as if he had suffered an evil, as unfitting. He still asks for help, reaching for externals as things preferred, not as goods ("I wished for your help, not your pity").
stoic_reason: Property, office and reputation are not up to us, and good and evil lie only in moral purpose (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). He assents to no passion of grief over the loss (R2, R4). He still seeks help, which is by nature preferable, without begging as though his good depended on it (Discourses 2.10), so the act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R5).

self: You, an old man back from exile who vowed to pass the rest of your life in quiet and tranquillity, receive letters from Caesar before entering Rome, forget all, and add one piece of business to another.

chapter: *Against those who eagerly seek preferment at Rome.*
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students, recounting his own exchange with the man
source_quote: Before he entered the city, he was met by letters from Caesar, and as soon as he received them, he forgot all, and ever after has added one piece of business to another.
source_verdict: I wish that I were now by his side to remind him of what he said when he was passing this way, and to tell him how much better a seer I am than he is.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats Caesar's favour and the office and business it offers, which are externals not up to him, as a good worth having. He abandons the tranquillity he had vowed as soon as the impression arrives. The words that suggest this: 'vowing to pass the rest of his life in quiet and tranquillity', 'receive letters from Caesar', 'forget all', and 'add one piece of business to another'.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R2, his sudden reversal, 'forgetting all' at a letter from Caesar, reads as assent to the impression that office and favour are goods. This is the craving for things not under our control that makes a man 'changed and tossed to and fro' and subordinate to those who can grant them (Discourses 1.4; Handbook 19). It is not a reasoned taking-up of a role's duty (R6), since nothing in the scene suggests duty rather than appetite for business and favour.

source_quote: Thrasea used to say, I would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow.
source_lesson: This it is to have studied what a man ought to study; to have made desire, aversion, free from hindrance, and free from all that a man would avoid.
source_verdict: If you choose death as the heavier misfortune, how great is the folly of your choice? But if, as the lighter, who has given you the choice? Will you not study to be content with that which has been given to you?
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats banishment, which is not up to him, as an evil so great that death is better. The vignette shows this in "would rather be killed to-day than banished to-morrow". Ranking two externals this sharply, with no stated reason, points to an aversion to exile rather than indifference to it. "As his settled choice" shows the judgement is assented to, not a passing reaction.
stoic_reason: Exile and death are both among the things not under our control (Handbook 1), so judging exile a dreadful evil is the kind of judgement that disturbs men (Handbook 5) and is a fault once it is his settled choice (R1, R2). It is not a first movement (R3, R7). He would act well only if he were calmly preferring one indifferent to another for a reasonable cause, and the scene gives no such cause (R1).

source_verdict: Priscus Helvidius also saw this, and acted conformably. ... Why, what else than this, that it is conspicuous in the toga as purple, and is displayed also as a fine example to all other things?
stoic_judgement: He treats doing the work of his role, going into the senate and saying what he thinks right, as what is up to him and good. He treats the emperor's threat of death as not up to him and not an evil that should move his choice. The vignette shows this in: "so long as he is a member he must go in and say what he thinks right."
stoic_reason: The office itself is not up to him, but while he holds it he acts on what the role of senator asks (Discourses 2.10; R6). He refuses to assent to the impression that death, an external, is something dreadful (Handbook 5; R1, R2). So the act proceeds from correct judgements and is well done.

chapter: What is the law of life.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking to the teacher who had arranged a young man's reading of hypothetical arguments
source_quote: the teacher who had suggested the reading was laughing at the reader
source_lesson: This then is the beginning of philosophy, a man's perception of the state of his ruling faculty; for when a man knows that it is weak, then he will not employ it on things of the greatest difficulty.
source_verdict: You are laughing at yourself: you did not prepare the young man nor did you ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters; but perhaps, you are only employing him as a reader.
stoic_judgement: The teacher treats the young man's failure as something to laugh at, as if the fault were the student's. In truth the fault comes from his own neglect: he 'did not prepare him nor ascertain whether he was able to understand these matters,' yet he is 'laughing at the young man he set to read hypothetical arguments.'
stoic_reason: By his role as teacher (R6, Discourses 2.10) he owed the student preparation and an assessment of what he could handle. He omitted that appropriate act (Arius 11a), then mocked the student instead of seeing his own part in the failure, which is a judgement contrary to correct reason (R1). The laughter is a deliberate response to a situation he set up, not a first movement (R3), so 'neither' gets little weight (R7).

This is shown by 'embracing the knees of a wealthy man' (supplication), 'complaining that he has only one and a half million denarii' and 'a vast fortune, remaining'.
stoic_reason: Complaining of want amid a vast fortune, and abasing himself before one who can procure more, shows assent to the judgement that property is a good and its loss an evil: a craving and grief over externals. That is acting badly even though no wrong is done to anyone (R1, R2; Handbook 1, 5; Discourses 1.4: he who craves things not under his control 'must end by subordinating himself to others').

chapter: That we ought not to be angry with the errors \(faults\) of others.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting his own experience to his listeners
source_quote: hearing a noise at the door, I ran down, and found that the lamp had been carried off. I reflected that he who had taken the lamp had done nothing strange. What then? To-morrow, I said, you will find an earthen lamp: for a man only loses that which he has.
source_reason: for a man only loses that which he has.
source_lesson: Why then are you troubled? for we only lose those things, we have only pains about those things which we possess.
source_verdict: Why then are you troubled? for we only lose those things, we have only pains about those things which we possess.
stoic_judgement: He treats the iron lamp as an external that was never truly his own good. Its loss is no evil to him, so the thief has done nothing to wonder at or be angry about. The vignette shows this in his calmly planning to get 'an earthen lamp tomorrow' and in 'the thief did nothing strange, for a man only loses that which he has.'
stoic_reason: The lamp is property, not under our control (Handbook 1), and only material for moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). He refuses the judgement that he has been harmed or insulted (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18, 'what ground is left for you to be angry'), and he still sensibly provides for a lamp, a preferred indifferent (Discourses 2.10). So by R1 and R2 the act proceeds from correct judgement and is done well (R5).

self: You, having sold your shoemaker as good for nothing, now, after he has become Caesar's shoemaker, ask, “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” and consult with him about something.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.19.19–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should behave to tyrants.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: You should have seen what respect Epaphroditus paid to him: “How does the good Felicion do, I pray?” Then if any of us asked, “What is master \(Epaphroditus\) doing?” the answer was, “He is consulting about something with Felicion.”
source_lesson: This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
source_verdict: Had he not sold the man as good for nothing? Who then made him wise all at once? This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
stoic_judgement: He treats Felicion's new nearness to Caesar, and the favour or influence it might bring, as a good worth courting. He also treats Felicion's worth as following his office rather than his character. The scene suggests this: the man who sold him 'as good for nothing' now calls him 'the good Felicion' and consults him only after he 'has become Caesar's shoemaker'. Nothing in Felicion is said to have changed except his place.
stoic_reason: Office and reputation are not up to us (Handbook 1). By judging another's office a good to be won, he 'must end by subordinating himself to others... who are able to procure or prevent these things that he craves' (Discourses 1.4). Changing his praise to suit what he hopes to gain is acting from a bad judgement (R1), not an honest reassessment.

So neglecting his office cannot be ruled out, and no single reading is clearly most likely.

self: When the ruler threatens you with death, you say to him, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you," for beyond the poor body no one has any power over you.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.25.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a lecture, citing Demetrius's reply to Nero
source_quote: Demetrius said to Nero, "You threaten me with death, but nature threatens you."
source_reason: and as to the last garment, that is the poor body, no one has any power over me beyond this
source_lesson: If I set my admiration on the poor body, I have given myself up to be a slave: if on my little possessions, I also make myself a slave: for I immediately make it plain with what I may be caught; as if the snake draws in his head, I tell you to strike that part of him which be guards; and do you be assured that whatever part you choose to guard, that part your master will attack.
source_verdict: If I set my admiration on the poor body, I have given myself up to be a slave: if on my little possessions, I also make myself a slave ... Remembering this whom will you still flatter or fear?
stoic_judgement: He treats death and the body as outside his control and not an evil, and his own moral purpose as the only thing that is his, which the ruler cannot touch. The scene shows this directly: "for beyond the poor body no one has any power over him", and his calm reply that death awaits the ruler too ("nature threatens you").
stoic_reason: The act comes from the correct judgement that body and life are not up to us and that death is nothing dreadful, only the judgement that it is dreadful (Handbook 1, 5; Discourses 1.1). So he feels no assented fear and is acting well (R1, R2), and what he shows is endurance in the face of fear of death (R8).

The words that show it: "begin to be angry and weep for a girl, forgetting that he is at Troy not to get mistresses, but to fight."

His forgetting why he is at Troy shows assent rather than a mere first movement (R3), and it neglects what his role as foremost warrior asks (R6; Discourses 2.10).
