'Little suit about a bit of land' and the taunt 'it is you rather than I who are on your trial' suggest a pose, a show of indifference, rather than plain indifference.
stoic_reason: Not begging is right, since the verdict is not under his control (Handbook 1). But his role as a litigant in a small dispute asks for a plain, fitting close (R6; Discourses 2.10). Taunting the judges, when he has already won the argument, most likely comes from vanity about seeming free, which is a judgement about reputation (R1, R2). If his indifference is genuine and unforced, the act would be well done.

other: You see a philosopher refuse a man asking for letters of recommendation, saying the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though he write ten thousand times.
self: You refuse a man asking you for letters of recommendation, saying the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though you write ten thousand times.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.3.1–2 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To those who recommend persons to philosophers.
speaker: Epictetus, recounting Diogenes' reply to a man who asked him for a letter of recommendation
source_quote: DIOGENES said well to one who asked from him letters of recommendation, “That you are a man, he said, he will know as soon as he sees you; and he will know whether you are good or bad, if he is by experience skilful to distinguish the good and the bad; but if he is without experience, he will never know, if I write to him ten thousand times.”
source_reason: he will know whether you are good or bad, if he is by experience skilful to distinguish the good and the bad; but if he is without experience, he will never know, if I write to him ten thousand times.
source_lesson: We ought then in life also to have some skill as in the case of silver coin that a man may be able to say like the judge of silver, Bring me any drachma and I will test it.
source_verdict: DIOGENES said well to one who asked from him letters of recommendation
stoic_judgement: He holds that a man's good or bad character is shown only to a judge skilled by experience, and that letters cannot supply it, so to write one would be useless or misleading. The vignette suggests this in: 'the recipient will know whether he is good or bad if by experience skilful to distinguish them, and never otherwise, though he write ten thousand times.'
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a stated and correct judgement (R1): whether another person sees the petitioner as good is not up to the writer. A reputation that rests on letters is an external, and refusing to vouch falsely fits his role as a philosopher (R6). Nothing in the scene shows contempt or a passion behind the refusal, though a reader might wonder whether kindness required some other help.

other: You see a philosopher facing trial, reminded by a friend to prepare for it, reply that he has been preparing for it all his life, for he has never done anything unjust in his private or public life.
self: You are facing trial, and when a friend reminds you to prepare for it, you reply that you have been preparing for it all your life, for you have never done anything unjust in your private or public life.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.2.8–9 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, citing Socrates
source_quote: I have maintained that which was in my own power. ... I have never done anything unjust either in my private or in my public life.
source_lesson: For if you wish to maintain a will conformable to nature, you have every security, every facility, you have no troubles.
source_verdict: Only do not intreat; but do not also say, ‘I do not intreat;’ unless there is a fit occasion to irritate purposely the judges, as was the case with Socrates.
stoic_judgement: He treats his own just conduct, which is up to him, as the only real preparation and defence, and the court's verdict, which is not up to him, as something he need not anxiously prepare for. The words that show it: 'he has been preparing for it all his life, for he has never done anything unjust in his private or public life.'
stoic_reason: He places his good in his moral purpose and the choices behind his acts, not in the external outcome of the trial (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). He shows no anxiety, unlike the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13, R2). His reply proceeds from a correct judgement, so it is well done (Discourses 4.8, R1, R5).

other: You see a man on trial for his life using pleasantry in court, asking his accuser who can believe there are mules but not asses, with chains, banishment, a draught of poison and his children's orphaning at stake.
self: You are on trial for your life and use pleasantry in court, asking your accuser who can believe there are mules but not asses, with chains, banishment, a draught of poison and your children's orphaning at stake.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.5.18–20 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How magnanimity is consistent with care.
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to his students
source_quote: Socrates then knew how to play at ball. How? By using pleasantry in the court where he was tried.
source_lesson: So we should do: we must employ all the care of the players, but show the same indifference about the ball.
source_verdict: but still he did play and threw the ball skilfully.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats chains, banishment, death by poison and his children's orphaning as things not up to him, and so not evils to dread. What is up to him is how he conducts his defence, and he conducts it calmly and pointedly. This is shown by his 'using pleasantry in court' while 'on trial for his life', with 'chains, banishment, a draught of poison and his children's orphaning at stake', and by aiming a reasoned quip at his accuser ('who can believe there are mules but not asses').
stoic_reason: Body, life and family fortunes are not under our control (Handbook 1), so a man who does not judge them dreadful is not disturbed by them (Handbook 5). His composure and wit, while he still makes his defence, are best read as coming from that correct judgement and not from an assented fear (R1, R2). His role as defendant is still fulfilled (R6). A smaller reading of flippancy that neglects a duty is possible but not suggested by the scene.

other: You see a condemned philosopher, about to drink the poison, excuse the jailor who had charge of him in prison and is weeping, and say, "How generously he laments over us."
self: You, a condemned philosopher about to drink the poison, excuse the jailor who has charge of you in prison and is weeping, and say, "How generously he laments over us."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.29.65–66 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, How generously he laments over us.
source_lesson: No, but we ought to accommodate ourselves to the ignorant \(τοῖς ἰδιώταις\) and to say: “This man recommends to me that which he thinks good for himself: I excuse him.”
source_verdict: For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, How generously he laments over us.
source_missing: Socrates did not lecture the jailor with the philosophical view that weeping over death is wrong (the reason the women had been sent away). He kept that teaching for the friends who could understand it and treated the jailor as a child.
stoic_judgement: He treats the jailor's part in his imprisonment as no wrong done to him, and the jailor's tears as goodwill to be acknowledged, not blamed. He does not treat his own coming death as an evil: he is 'about to drink the poison' yet turns his attention to excusing another and praising his feeling ('How generously he laments over us').
stoic_reason: He does not blame the jailor, who acts from what appears right to him in his role (Handbook 42, 20; R6), and he answers the man's affection kindly in words (Handbook 16; Discourses 1.11; R4). His composure at the point of death suggests he does not judge death dreadful (Handbook 5). Read most likely, this is an act from correct judgements: acting well (R1, R5).

other: You see a man of letters who had once been detected in adultery in the city say, "What then, are not women common by nature? I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus."
self: You, a man of letters who had once been detected in adultery in the city, say, "What then, are not women common by nature? I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus."
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.4.1–3 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: Against a person who had once been detected in adultery.
speaker: Epictetus, addressing a man of letters present in his audience who had once been detected in adultery
source_quote: had once been detected in adultery in the city
source_reason: What then, are not women common by nature? ... But I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus.
source_lesson: Understand Archedemus then, and be an adulterer, and faithless, and instead of a man, be a wolf or an ape: for what is the difference?
source_verdict: They do not, because you are bad and useless.
stoic_judgement: He treats his own appetite, and taking another man's wife, as permissible and good for him. He uses learned doctrine to excuse it rather than to correct it. This is shown by the words "detected in adultery" and "are not women common by nature? I am a man of letters and understand Archedemus."
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a bad judgement (R1): he twists a school doctrine to justify a past wrong instead of judging rightly what is due to others. The judgement shown is that the fault was no wrong at all. That is an error, contrary to right reason, against what his role as a neighbour and citizen asks (R6). Being ready with arguments while doing wrong is the failure Handbook 52 names.

other: You see a woman indulging her passion and taking vengeance on her husband rather than sparing her children, because she thinks this more profitable.
self: You indulge your passion and take vengeance on your husband rather than sparing your children, because you think this more profitable.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.28.7–9; repeated 2.17.19–22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men.*
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his hearers
source_quote: to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband ... than to spare her children
source_reason: She thought that to indulge her passion and take vengeance on her husband was more profitable than to spare her children.
source_lesson: Why then are you angry with the unhappy woman that she has been bewildered about the most important things, and is become a viper instead of human creature? And why not, if it is possible, rather pity, as we pity the blind and the lame, so those who are blinded and maimed in the faculties which are supreme?
source_verdict: It was so; but she was deceived.
stoic_judgement: She treats gratifying her passion by revenge on her husband as a greater good than her children's safety. The vignette shows this in 'indulging her passion', 'taking vengeance' and 'because she thinks this more profitable'.
stoic_reason: Her act proceeds from a bad judgement: she assents to the passion and holds that revenge is profitable (R1, R2; Discourses 4.8, Handbook 42, the deceived is the one who suffers). She sacrifices what her role as mother asks of her (R6; Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10).

other: You see a warrior who, when he was going to strike the enemy, checks himself when he hears the trumpet sounding a retreat, because it seems better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination.
self: You are going to strike the enemy and check yourself when you hear the trumpet sounding a retreat, because it seems better to you to obey the general's command than to follow your own inclination.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.6.15 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: when he was going to strike the enemy checked himself when he heard the trumpet sounding a retreat
source_reason: it seemed better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination.
source_lesson: But not one of us chooses, even when necessity summons, readily to obey it, but weeping and groaning we suffer what we do suffer, and we call them 'circumstances.'
source_verdict: But not one of us chooses, even when necessity summons, readily to obey it, but weeping and groaning we suffer what we do suffer, and we call them 'circumstances.'
stoic_judgement: He treats obeying his general, as his role as a soldier requires, as better than acting on his own impulse to strike. The vignette states this: "because it seems better to him to obey the general's command than to follow his own inclination."
stoic_reason: The act comes from a stated, correct judgement about what his role as a soldier asks (R1, R6; Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10). He checks an impulse with reason instead of being carried by it, which is acting well as one making progress (R5). Retreating from the fight is not a passion or a mere first movement; his urge to strike is mastered, not assented to (R2, R3).

other: You see a woman intending to send by a vessel a month's provisions to her friend in banishment, saying she would rather the emperor should seize all than that she should not send it.
self: You intend to send by a vessel a month's provisions to your friend in banishment, saying you would rather the emperor should seize all than that you should not send it.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.7.8 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we ought to use divination.
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse to his students
source_quote: who intended to send by a vessel a month's provisions to Gratilla in her banishment
source_reason: I would rather, she replied, that Domitian should seize all than that I should not send it.
source_lesson: If then I must expose myself to danger for a friend, and if it is my duty even to die for him, what need have I then for divination?
source_verdict: made a good answer to him who said that Domitian would seize what she sent
stoic_judgement: She treats sending the provisions, an act of faithfulness to her banished friend, as the thing that is hers to do. She treats the provisions themselves, and whether the emperor seizes them, as not worth failing her duty over. The words that show this: 'intending to send ... to her friend in banishment' and 'she would rather the emperor should seize all than that she should not send it'.
stoic_reason: Her act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8). The provisions are property, and their seizure is not up to her. Her choice to keep faith with a friend is up to her, and she does not let fear of losing an external stop her (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.29). Care for a friend, done with reason, is affectionate and reasonable, 'right and good' (R4, Discourses 1.11), and it fits the duties of friendship (R6).

other: You see one of a teacher's companions, on the third day of abstaining from food, holding to his resolve, made for no reason, to starve himself to death, saying, 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
self: You are on the third day of abstaining from food, having resolved for no reason to starve yourself to death, and when your teacher asks why, you say, 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.15.4–13 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To or against those who obstinately persist in what they have determined.
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, recounting how he went to confront his companion
source_quote: resolved to starve himself to death
source_reason: We ought to keep to our determinations.
source_lesson: We ought to keep not to all our determinations, but to those which are right
source_verdict: Then while you are committing murder and destroying a man who has done no wrong, do you say that you ought to abide by your determinations?
stoic_judgement: He treats sticking to a resolution as good in itself, whether or not the resolution is sound, and so treats his own death as something to pursue for no reason. The vignette shows this in 'holding to his resolve, made for no reason, to starve himself to death' and in his saying 'We ought to keep to our determinations.'
stoic_reason: Only the act that comes from correct judgements is well done (Discourses 4.8). His act comes from a rash assent, a resolve the scene says was made for no reason, that he never tested (the third field, Discourses 3.2). Being sincere about a wrong view does not make it right (Handbook 42), so this is acting badly (R1, R2). Days of steady fasting are not a first movement or an act reason neither urges nor forbids, so 'neither' does not fit (R7).

other: You see a philosopher lying down beside a beautiful young man, abstaining from touching him and mocking his beauty instead of yielding to it.
self: You lie down beside a beautiful young man, abstaining from touching him and mocking his beauty instead of yielding to it.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.18.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should struggle against appearances.
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse to his students
source_quote: lying down with Alcibiades, and mocking his beauty
source_lesson: By placing these objects on the other side you will conquer the appearance: you will not be drawn away by it.
source_verdict: consider what a victory he at last found that he had gained over himself; what an Olympian victory; in what number he stood from Hercules; so that, by the Gods, one may justly salute him, Hail, wondrous man, you who have conquered not these sorry boxers and pancratiasts, nor yet those who are like them, the gladiators.
stoic_judgement: He treats the young man's beauty, and the pleasure of yielding to it, as an external that is not a good worth having. He keeps his choice in his own control rather than being carried away by the impression. Shown by "abstaining from touching him" and "mocking his beauty instead of yielding to it".
stoic_reason: He tests the impression of beauty and refuses assent to the judgement that its enjoyment is a good, so his desire stays with what is up to him (Handbook 1, Discourses 3.2, the first field). Epictetus himself holds up this kind of victory over an attractive impression as training (Discourses 2.18). By R1 and R2 the act comes from a correct judgement and is well done, and restraint of appetite is temperance (R8).

other: You see a king anxious when he is going to meet a philosopher, for he wishes to please the philosopher.
self: You are a king, and you are anxious when you are going to meet a philosopher, for you wish to please him.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.13.14–15 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse, with an interlocutor answering him in the application that follows the case
source_quote: But Antigonus was anxious when he was going to meet Zeno
source_reason: for he wished to please Zeno
source_lesson: But Zeno did not want to please Antigonus; for no man who is skilled in any art wishes to please one who has no such skill.
source_verdict: no good man laments or groans or weeps, no good man is pale and trembles, or says, How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?
stoic_judgement: The king treats pleasing the philosopher, the philosopher's approval, as a good he must win, though it is not up to him. The vignette shows this in "anxious when he is going to meet a philosopher, for he wishes to please the philosopher."
stoic_reason: By Discourses 2.13, anxiety shows a man wants something outside his control. Like the singer who wants applause, the king craves another's good opinion, so this is an assented passion and he is acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). The stated motive and the ongoing anxiety point to assent rather than a mere first movement (R3, R7).

other: You see a man who is a guest in another man's house carry off his host's wife, as it appeared to him to do, and she follows him.
self: You, a guest in another man's house, carry off your host's wife, as it appears to you to do, and she follows you.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.28.12,23; repeated 2.22.23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with an interlocutor (his Discourse)
source_quote: It appeared to Alexander to carry off the wife of Menelaus: it appeared to Helene to follow him.
source_lesson: So then all these great and dreadful deeds have this origin, in the appearance (opinion)? Yes, this origin and no other.
source_verdict: now the ruin of Alexander was when he lost the character of modesty, fidelity, regard to hospitality, and to decency.
modernised: [{"source": "the wife of Menelaus", "vignette": "his host's wife", "why": "A reader today would not know that Menelaus was Alexander's host. Without that, the breach of hospitality and fidelity on which the author's verdict turns would be lost."}]
stoic_judgement: He treats possessing his host's wife as a good worth breaking faith with his host for. The vignette shows this in "a guest in another man's house carry off his host's wife, as it appeared to him to do": he acts on what seems good to him, and the act is taking what is his host's.
stoic_reason: He acts from what appears good to him, but the appearance is false. A guest who betrays his host's trust and takes his wife has treated an external, another's wife and the pleasure of having her, as his good. So the act proceeds from a bad judgement and is badly done (Discourses 4.8, R1; Handbook 42: a sincere judgement can still be wrong, and the one deceived is the one harmed). He also violates what the role of guest asks (R6). Her following him does not change his judgement or his role.

other: You see a philosopher, when an earthquake happens, imagine that the city is going to fall on him.
self: When an earthquake happens, you, a philosopher, imagine that the city is going to fall on you.
contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.60) | The source's author judges it badly; Epictetus's framing gives neutral
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.16.23 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we do not strive to use our opinions about good and evil.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking to his students, using his own reactions as the example
source_quote: when an earthquake shall happen, I imagine that the city is going to fall on me
source_lesson: What then are the things which are heavy on us and disturb us? What else than opinions?
source_verdict: Consequently through want of discipline we are always adding something to the appearance and representing things to be greater than what they are.
stoic_judgement: Most likely a sudden impression that something terrible is looming ('imagine that the city is going to fall on him') at the moment the earthquake strikes. The vignette does not show him assenting to it as an evil, acting in panic, or treating his death as the worst thing. A lesser reading is that he judges being crushed a dreadful evil, which would be the passion of fear.
stoic_reason: An earthquake is the kind of sudden peril of fragment 9, where 'the mind of even the wise man cannot help but be disturbed' by swift, unconsidered motions. An impression of danger, without assent that the danger is an evil, is a first movement and so neither (R3, R7). If he assents that being crushed is dreadful, that is fear, an assented passion (R2, Handbook 5), which is why 'badly' keeps real weight.

other: You see a man seeking the costly priesthood of Augustus because those who draw up agreements will write his name, his name will remain, and he will wear a crown of gold.
self: You seek the costly priesthood of Augustus because those who draw up agreements will write your name, your name will remain, and you will wear a crown of gold.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.19.26–29 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we should behave to tyrants.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a man who is interested in the priesthood of Augustus
source_quote: A person was talking to me to-day about the priesthood of Augustus ... But he replies, "Those who draw up agreements will write my name." ... My name will remain. ... But I shall wear a crown of gold.
source_reason: "Those who draw up agreements will write my name." ... My name will remain. ... But I shall wear a crown of gold.
source_lesson: This is an instance of valuing something else than the things which depend on the will.
source_verdict: "Man, let the thing alone: you will spend much for no purpose." ... If you desire a crown at all, take a crown of roses and put it on, for it will be more elegant in appearance.
stoic_judgement: He treats reputation and honour, which are not up to him, as goods worth great cost. The vignette states his reasons: 'those who draw up agreements will write his name, his name will remain, and he will wear a crown of gold.'
stoic_reason: The stated reason is the judgement that reputation and office are good, though Handbook 1 lists them among things not under our control. Handbook 19 says one who knows the good should not wish for office but to be free, and Discourses 1.4 says one who craves such things cannot be free. So the choice proceeds from a bad judgement and is badly done (R1, R2).

other: You see a man on a voyage look down on the deep sea and round on it, seeing no land, and he is out of his mind, imagining he must drink up all this water if wrecked.
self: You are on a voyage, look down on the deep sea and round on it and see no land, and you are out of your mind, imagining you must drink up all this water if you are wrecked.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.16.22 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: That we do not strive to use our opinions about good and evil.
speaker: Epictetus, speaking in his own person in a lecture
source_quote: when I am on a voyage and look down on the deep sea, or look round on it and see no land, I am out of my mind and imagine that I must drink up all this water if I am wrecked, and it does not occur to me that three pints are enough
source_lesson: What then disturbs me? The sea? No, but my opinion.
source_verdict: Consequently through want of discipline we are always adding something to the appearance and representing things to be greater than what they are.
source_missing: The vignette leaves out that it does not occur to him that three pints of water would be enough to drown him. That oversight is exactly how he magnifies the appearance beyond what it is.
stoic_judgement: He treats being wrecked and drowning, which is not up to him, as a terrible evil, and assents to an exaggerated impression of it: "he is out of his mind, imagining he must drink up all this water if wrecked."
stoic_reason: Fear is the judgement that something outside our control is dreadful. Here it is not a sudden first movement: he looks round, dwells on the impression and is carried away by it. So it is an assented passion and he acts badly (R2, Handbook 5, Discourses 2.13). It is not a mere start of fright (R3, R7).

other: You see a provincial governor, Caesar's friend and deputy, cry out and spring up from his seat in the theatre, his slaves calling out, because he wishes an actor to be crowned.
self: You, a provincial governor and Caesar's friend and deputy, cry out and spring up from your seat in the theatre, your slaves calling out, because you wish an actor to be crowned.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.4.1–12 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: Against a person who showed his partizanship in an unseemly way in a theatre.
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with the governor of Epirus
source_quote: having shown his favour to an actor in an unseemly way ... and that he was vexed at those who blamed him
source_reason: But I wish Sophron to be crowned.
source_lesson: But in public do not claim more than your due, nor attempt to appropriate to yourself what belongs to all.
source_verdict: for if it is not right to show partizanship in this way, do not do so yourself; and if it is right, why are you angry if they followed your example?
stoic_judgement: He treats the actor's being crowned, something not up to him, as a good he must have and will strive for in public. His desire is shown by "cry out and spring up from his seat", "his slaves calling out" and "because he wishes an actor to be crowned".
stoic_reason: Like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), he craves an external outside his control and acts from that assented passion (R1, R2). His role as Caesar's deputy and governor calls for orderly conduct befitting the office, not a partisan's outcry (Discourses 2.10; R6). Rising, crying out and setting his slaves shouting is a sustained, willed act, not a brief first movement (R3, R7).

other: You see a man, born of the same mother and father as his brother and brought up together with him, quarrel with him about the royal power and tell him, 'I will place myself opposite and try to kill you.'
self: You, born of the same mother and father as your brother and brought up together with him, quarrel with him about the royal power and tell him, 'I will place myself opposite and try to kill you.'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.13–14 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to his pupils
source_quote: But when a quarrel rose between them about the royal power, as between dogs about a bit of meat ... I will place myself opposite and try to kill you. ... I also wish to do the same. Such are the wishes that they utter.
source_reason: about the royal power
source_lesson: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interest.
source_verdict: If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free: do not name them even men, if you have any judgment.
stoic_judgement: He treats the royal power, an external not up to him, as a good great enough to kill his own brother for. The vignette shows this in "quarrel with him about the royal power" and "I will place myself opposite and try to kill you," said to one "born of the same mother and father ... and brought up together with him."
stoic_reason: He craves a thing not under his control (Handbook 1, 19; Discourses 1.4: one who craves externals 'can be neither faithful nor free'). Against what the role of brother asks (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10), he resolves to kill his brother for it. This is an assented passion acted on, not a first movement, so it is acting badly (R1, R2, R6).

other: You see a ruler, when his dear friend died, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned.
self: When your dear friend dies, you, a ruler, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.17 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his hearers
source_quote: Alexander ordered the temples of Aes- culapius to be burned
source_reason: when his dear friend died
source_lesson: For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest.
source_verdict: For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest.
modernised: [{"source": "Aesculapius", "vignette": "Aesculapius, the god of healing", "why": "A reader today may not know Aesculapius was the god of healing, and so would miss that the ruler is striking at the god he holds to blame for the friend's death."}]
stoic_judgement: He treats his friend's death as a great evil, and the god of healing as at fault for not preventing it and so deserving punishment. The words that show it: 'when his dear friend died, order the temples of Aesculapius, the god of healing, to be burned.' Choosing the healing god's temples as the target suggests he blames the god for the death.
stoic_reason: Death is not up to us and is nothing dreadful; the judgement that it is dreadful is the fault (Handbook 5). Here grief assented to has become anger acted on: a deliberate order, not a first movement (R2, R3). Burning temples is also impious and harms what belongs to others, so it is not the sympathy or affection 'with reason' that R4 allows.

other: You see a sophist, at whom the philosopher Diogenes has pointed by stretching out his middle finger, wild with rage.
self: You are a sophist, and when the philosopher Diogenes points you out by stretching out his middle finger at you, you are wild with rage.
contested_note: The source's author judges it well; Epictetus's framing gives vice
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.2.11–12 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *In what a man ought to be exercised who has made proficiency; and that we neglect the chief things.*
speaker: Epictetus, addressing a pupil
source_quote: when the man was wild with rage
source_lesson: For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
source_verdict: For a man is not shown by the finger, as a stone or a piece of wood; but when any person shows the man's principles, then he shows him as a man.
source_missing: The vignette leaves out the purpose of the gesture. Diogenes made it to provoke the sophist's reaction, and once the man raged he said, "This is the certain person: I have pointed him out to you." His point was that the man's angry response, not the finger, exposed his principles and character.
stoic_judgement: The sophist treats Diogenes' gesture, an insult to his reputation, which is not up to him, as a real harm done to him, and he assents to anger at it. The vignette shows this in "wild with rage" in response to Diogenes "stretching out his middle finger" at him.
stoic_reason: Under Handbook 20 it is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your own judgement that he does. Under Discourses 1.18 there is no ground for anger, since one's moral purpose is untouched. Rage that is "wild" is an assented passion, not a passing first movement, so it is acting badly (R2, with R3 considered and not applied).

other: You see the most reputed philosopher among the Romans, vexed with his own friends as if suffering something intolerable, cry, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is," pointing to another philosopher.
self: You, the most reputed philosopher among the Romans, vexed with your own friends as if suffering something intolerable, cry, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is," pointing to another philosopher.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.8.7 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: How we must exercise ourselves against appearances (φαντασίας).
speaker: Epictetus, telling his audience of an incident at which he was present
source_quote: being vexed with his own friends and as if he was suffering something intolerable said, "I cannot bear it, you are killing me: you will make me such as that man is;" pointing to me
source_lesson: Hear how the Romans feel towards philosophers, if you would like to know.
source_verdict: Affliction is a thing which depends on the will: it is an evil.
stoic_judgement: He treats what his friends are doing as a real and intolerable harm. He believes they can corrupt his character against his will and make him like the other philosopher. The vignette shows this in "vexed with his own friends as if suffering something intolerable", "I cannot bear it, you are killing me" and "you will make me such as that man is".
stoic_reason: His concern for his own character is the right concern. But his vexation assents to the impression that others, who are not up to him, can harm his moral purpose, and Epictetus says no one but ourselves can do that (Handbook 1, 5, 20; Discourses 1.29). So this is an assented passion and he acts badly (R2, R1). The small weight on 'well' covers a reading in which his outburst is a sound refusal of something corrupting.

other: You see a wife who has lived long with her husband and is the mother of his many children let a necklace come between them, through her opinion about such things.
self: You, a wife who has lived long with your husband and are the mother of his many children, let a necklace come between you, through your opinion about such things.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 2.22.32–33 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse on friendship, answering an imagined objection about a wife of long standing
source_quote: But a necklace came between them:
source_reason: and what is a necklace? It is the opinion about such things.
source_lesson: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul.
source_verdict: That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.
stoic_judgement: She treats the necklace, an external not up to her, as a good worth more than her bond with her husband and children. The vignette says she lets it 'come between them, through her opinion about such things.'
stoic_reason: It is not the necklace that divides them but her judgement about it (Handbook 5). Taking an external for a good leads her to neglect what her role as long-standing wife and mother asks, so the act proceeds from a bad judgement and is badly done (R1, R2, R6; Discourses 1.29, 4.8).

other: You see a philosopher, half asleep, answer a king who stands by him quoting Homer's line 'A man a councillor should not sleep all night' with 'The people's guardian and so full of cares.'
self: You, half asleep, answer a king who stands by you quoting Homer's line 'A man a councillor should not sleep all night' with 'The people's guardian and so full of cares.'
contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.55)
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.92 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in discourse with a young man who is considering the Cynic life
source_quote: in reply to Alexander, who stood by him when he was sleeping, and quoted Homer's line ... he answered, when he was half asleep, ... The people's guardian and so full of cares.
source_lesson: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
source_verdict: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
stoic_judgement: He most likely judges that the Homeric duty of sleepless care belongs to the role of 'the people's guardian', which is the king's role and not his, and that the king's rebuke is not his concern. Shown by his reply, which completes the king's quoted line ('A man a councillor should not sleep all night') with its next line ('The people's guardian and so full of cares'), turning the rebuke back onto the king's own role while he himself stays at rest.
stoic_reason: By R6, each designation 'suggests the acts that are appropriate to it' (Discourses 2.10): the councillor's sleepless care is the king's duty, not a private man's. The king's opinion and power are not up to him, so he is not disturbed (Handbook 1, 20), and he answers calmly and frankly. This most likely proceeds from a correct judgement (R1), though the scene shows only a witty half-asleep reply, so some weight goes to 'neither'.

other: You see a man vexed that a flatterer, free from shame, has become rich, saying the unjust man has the advantage in money, though he himself would never lie with Sura for it and admits modesty is better than riches.
self: You are vexed that a flatterer, free from shame, has become rich, saying the unjust man has the advantage in money, though you would never lie with Sura for it and admit modesty is better than riches.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.17.4–5 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, recounting how he questioned a man vexed at Philostorgus's good fortune
source_quote: was vexed because Philostorgus was fortunate
source_reason: the unjust man has the advantage ... In money.
source_lesson: Remember then always and have in readiness the truth, that this is a law of nature, that the superior has an advantage over the inferior in that in which he is superior; and you will never be vexed.
source_verdict: Why are you vexed then, man, when you possess the better thing?
stoic_judgement: He treats the flatterer's wealth, an external not up to him, as a good he has been unfairly denied. The scene shows this in 'vexed that a flatterer ... has become rich' and 'saying the unjust man has the advantage in money'. His refusal to 'lie with Sura for it' and his admission that 'modesty is better than riches' show he holds the right principle in words, but his vexation shows he still assents to the impression that the money matters.
stoic_reason: Vexation at another's gain is an assented passion, the judgement that an external is good, and so is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2; Handbook 19, 'there is no place for either envy or jealousy'). Holding the correct argument while feeling from the wrong judgement fits Handbook 52, and his principled refusal does not cancel the faulty judgement he feels from (R1).

other: You see a Cynic in a fever, convinced that whatever he suffers it is Zeus who is exercising him, call to passers-by going to Olympia to see athletes fight, 'Miserable wretches, will you not stay and see the combat between a fever and a man?'
self: You, a Cynic in a fever, convinced that whatever you suffer it is Zeus who is exercising you, call to passers-by going to Olympia to see athletes fight, 'Miserable wretches, will you not stay and see the combat between a fever and a man?'
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.58–59 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, replying to a pupil inclined to Cynicism who asked what kind of person a Cynic ought to be
source_quote: Hear what Diogenes says to the passers by when he is in a fever, Miserable wretches, will you not stay? but are you going so long a journey to Olympia to see the destruction or the fight of athletes; and will you not choose to see the combat between a fever and a man?
source_reason: Is he not convinced that whatever he suffers, it is Zeus who is exercising him?
source_lesson: And is he who is trained to the contest and exercised by Zeus going to call out and to be vexed, he who is worthy to bear the sceptre of Diogenes?
source_verdict: Would such a man accuse God who sent him down as if God were treating him unworthily, a man who gloried in his circumstances, and claimed to be an example to those who were passing by?
stoic_judgement: He treats the fever as no evil but as training set by Zeus, a contest in which his own good lies in how he bears it. The words that show this: 'convinced that whatever he suffers it is Zeus who is exercising him', and 'the combat between a fever and a man'.
stoic_reason: The judgement behind his bearing is stated and correct: the body is not up to us, and a fever is material for the moral purpose, not an evil (Discourses 1.29, Handbook 1, 5). An act or feeling that proceeds from a correct judgement is well done (R1, Discourses 4.8), and for a Cynic, calling others to look at what is truly a contest fits his role (R6). There is a small chance the call to passers-by shows a wish for spectators, like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13), but the scene does not show that.

other: You see a Cynic philosopher, asked by a man, 'Are you the one who does not believe that there are gods?', reply, 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?'
self: You, a Cynic philosopher, are asked by a man, 'Are you the one who does not believe that there are gods?', and you reply, 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?'
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it: Epictetus's framing turns on whether the retort comes from the role's correct judgement (frank, pious correction) or from treating the imputation of atheism as an insult to repay (Handbook 20, 42). The vignette shows only the words, which fit both readings about equally. | no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.45)
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.22.91 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse on the Cynic character, answering a young man who is considering the Cynic life
source_quote: So Diogenes replied to one who said, Are you the Diogenes who does not believe that there are gods? And, how, replied Diogenes, can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?
source_reason: when I think that you are odious to the gods
source_lesson: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
source_verdict: There ought also to belong to the Cynic much natural grace and sharpness; and if this is not so, he is a stupid fellow, and nothing else; and he must have these qualities that he may be able readily and fitly to be a match for all circumstances that may happen.
stoic_judgement: The Cynic most likely treats the charge of disbelief as false and worth correcting: his reply 'How can this be when I think that you are odious to the gods?' takes the gods' existence for granted. He answers with a sharp rebuke of the questioner rather than a plain denial. The scene does not show whether this rebuke comes from a correct judgement in his role (the Cynic's frank correction of a man he thinks impious) or from treating the imputation as an insult to be returned.
stoic_reason: By R1 the verdict follows the judgement behind the retort. By R6, rebuking others may belong to the Cynic's role. But by Handbook 20 and 42, answering a perceived slight with a counter-slight would show the judgement that the man's words harmed him. The scene gives no clear sign which judgement he acts from, so neither reading is clearly most likely.

other: You see a father sail as far as Cassiope in winter with his son, the father himself accompanying his son on the voyage.
self: You sail as far as Cassiope in winter with your son, you yourself accompanying your son on the voyage.
contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.60)
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.7.3 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: To the administrator of the free cities who was an Epicurean.
speaker: Epictetus, questioning the visiting administrator of the free cities, who was an Epicurean
source_quote: Maximus sailed as far as Cassiope in winter \(or bad weather\) with his son, and accompanied him
source_lesson: For this reason Maximus acted foolishly if he made the voyage for any other reason than for the sake of the flesh, that is, for the sake of the best.
source_verdict: For this reason Maximus acted foolishly if he made the voyage for any other reason than for the sake of the flesh, that is, for the sake of the best.
source_missing: Why Maximus made the voyage: the interlocutor insists it was not to gratify the flesh ('Far be that from him'). Everything turns on this motive. The 'foolishly' verdict is an ironic reductio of Epicurean doctrine, which implies that Epictetus himself regards the voyage as rightly done.
stoic_judgement: The father most likely judges that caring for his son is his part as a father, and that it is worth the hardship and risk of a winter voyage. The scene shows this in 'sail as far as Cassiope in winter with his son' and 'the father himself accompanying his son'. The emphasis on 'himself' suggests he chose to go in person rather than send the boy off alone or with others.
stoic_reason: A father's designation suggests care for his child (Discourses 2.10, R6). Affection acted on with reason is 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11, R4), and enduring a winter sea for that duty fits courage as well as kindness. Read this way the act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R5). There is a lesser reading: an anxious father who cannot bear to let the boy go, treating the son's safety, which is not up to him, as a good he must secure (Discourses 2.13, R2). The scene gives no hint of that anxiety, so it gets lower probability.

other: You see a far-traveled man, parted from his wife, feeling a desire for his wife and weeping as he sits on a rock.
self: You are parted from your wife, and you feel a desire for her and weep as you sit on a rock.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.24.18–20 (Long; file edition 1890)
chapter: *That we ought not to be moved by a desire of those things which are not in our power.*
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing, answering an objection raised by an imagined student who quotes Homer
source_quote: Ulysses felt a desire for his wife and wept as he sat on a rock.
source_lesson: To desire then things which are impossible is to have a slavish character, and is foolish: it is the part of a stranger, of a man who fights against God in the only way that he can, by his opinions.
source_verdict: Or if Ulysses really wept, what was he else than an unhappy man? and what good man is unhappy? ... and if Ulysses did weep and lament, he was not a good man.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats being with his wife, which is not up to him, as a good he must have, and being apart from her as an evil. The scene suggests this: he is 'feeling a desire for his wife and weeping as he sits on a rock'. He is not caught by a sudden blow. He sits and weeps over a lasting absence.
stoic_reason: Desire aimed at something outside our control, held to and wept over, is an assented passion and so acting badly (R2; Handbook 1, Discourses 2.13). Affection for a wife is not itself the fault, and tears alone do not decide the label (R4). But a settled scene of longing reads more like grief assented to than an unwilled first movement (R3). That leaves some weight on 'neither'.

other: You see a man, sent by the tyrants to seize another man, refuse without even deliberating about the matter, because he thinks it a base action, knowing he must die for his refusal if it so happens.
self: You are sent by the tyrants to seize a man, and you refuse without even deliberating about the matter, because you think it a base action, knowing you must die for your refusal if it so happens.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.160–161 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in a discourse to his students
source_quote: when he was sent by the tyrants to seize Leon, he did not even deliberate about the matter
source_reason: because he thought that it was a base action ... for he intended to preserve something else, not his poor flesh, but his fidelity, his honourable character.
source_lesson: These are things which could not be assailed nor brought into subjection.
source_verdict: Socrates will not save his life by a base act; ... he who refused to obey the tyrants, ... It is not possible to save such a man's life by base acts, but he is saved by dying, not by running away.
stoic_judgement: He treats taking part in an unjust seizure as base, a ruin of his own moral purpose, and treats his own death as not an evil compared with that. Shown by: "refuse ... because he thinks it a base action, knowing he must die for his refusal" and "without even deliberating about the matter".
stoic_reason: The act comes from a stated correct judgement: the only evil is a bad moral purpose, and the body and life are not up to us. So the refusal is well done (R1, Discourses 4.8). Refusing a role-demand that requires a shameful act is appropriate (R6). Facing death for it without the passion of fear shows courage, and refusing to wrong another shows justice (R8).

other: You see a veteran who has seen much military service sending presents to a girl who hates him, and intreating her and weeping.
self: You, a veteran who has seen much military service, send presents to a girl who hates you, and intreat her and weep.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.19–23 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, addressing an interlocutor who claims to be free
source_quote: first of all went out by night, when Geta \(a slave\) does not venture out ... he sends presents to her who hates him, and intreats and weeps, and on the other hand having had a little success he is elated
source_lesson: Unhappy man, who are the slave even of a girl, and a worthless girl.
source_verdict: Unhappy man, who are the slave even of a girl, and a worthless girl.
source_missing: That he acts against his own will, driven by his passion: he himself admits that 'a worthless girl has enslaved me, me whom no enemy ever did.'
stoic_judgement: He treats the girl's love, which is not up to him, as a good he must have, and her hatred as an evil. The scene shows this: he is 'sending presents to a girl who hates him, and intreating her and weeping.' He keeps entreating someone who has already refused him, and pays to win what is not his to control.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R2 this is an assented passion. It is a desire for something outside his moral purpose, and so he 'must end by subordinating himself to others' who can grant or withhold what he craves (Discourses 1.4; cf. the singer craving applause, Discourses 2.13). The weeping comes with deliberate, repeated pleading and gifts, so it is not a mere first movement (R3, R4).

other: You see a man cast out shipwrecked go off to the young women to beg for necessaries, which is considered most shameful, relying on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
self: You are cast out shipwrecked and go off to the young women to beg for necessaries, which is considered most shameful, relying on your opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.26.33–34 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, discoursing to a pupil (addressed as 'you') who fears want and is ashamed of begging or of menial ways of getting food
source_quote: And when Ulysses was cast out shipwrecked, did want humiliate him, did it break his spirit? but how did he go off to the virgins to ask for necessaries, to beg which is considered most shameful?
source_reason: Not on reputation nor on wealth nor on the power of a magistrate, but on his own strength, that is, on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.
source_lesson: For these are the only things which make men free, which make them escape from hindrance, which raise the head (neck) of those who are depressed, which make them look with steady eyes on the rich and on tyrants.
source_verdict: And when Ulysses was cast out shipwrecked, did want humiliate him, did it break his spirit?
modernised: [{"source": "the virgins", "vignette": "the young women", "why": "Today 'virgins' points to sexual status, but the source only means unmarried young women. Readers might wrongly think that status matters to the act of begging."}]
stoic_judgement: He treats the shame others attach to begging, which concerns reputation and is not up to him, as no evil. He treats meeting his body's needs in his plight as a preferred thing to act for. The vignette shows this in 'which is considered most shameful, relying on his opinions about the things which are in our power and those which are not.'
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from the correct judgement that reputation and the opinions of others are not under our control, so it is well done (Discourses 4.8, Handbook 1; R1). He cleaves to what is naturally preferable, the necessaries of life, without the passion of shame or fear of disgrace (Discourses 2.10; R2, R5).

other: You see a philosopher, taken prisoner by pirates, reprove them for feeding their captives badly, for he has said that he can no longer be enslaved by any man.
self: You, taken prisoner by pirates, reprove them for feeding their captives badly, for you have said that you can no longer be enslaved by any man.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.115; related 3.24.66 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with a visitor
source_quote: when he was taken prisoner, how did he behave to the pirates? ... How did he reprove them for feeding badly their captives?
source_reason: he said that he could no longer be enslaved by any man
source_lesson: for this is really freedom.
source_verdict: And what was strange in this? for if his master had bought an exercise master, would he have employed him in the exercises of the palaestra as a servant or as a master? and sc if he had bought a physician or an architect. And so in every matter, it is absolutely necessary that he who has skill must be the superior of him who has not. Whoever then generally possesses the science of life, what else must he be than master?
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats his freedom as lying in his own moral purpose, not in his body or circumstances. So he judges captivity no evil and the pirates' power nothing to fear, while still treating decent food for the captives as a thing to be preferred and spoken up for. The words that show this are 'he has said that he can no longer be enslaved by any man' together with 'reprove them for feeding their captives badly', said while 'taken prisoner by pirates'.
stoic_reason: His body and his captivity are not under his control; only his use of impressions is (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.1). Because he does not treat the pirates' power as an evil, he can speak freely without fear (Handbook 20, Discourses 1.4 on not subordinating oneself to those who control externals). At the same time he acts for what is naturally preferable, food for the captives (Discourses 2.10). The act therefore most likely proceeds from correct judgements (R1, R5). There is a small chance the rebuke is vanity or a show of defiance (R2).

other: You see a philosopher, taken prisoner by pirates and sold as a slave, immediately tell his master that he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is, and how to bring up his children.
self: You, a philosopher taken prisoner by pirates and sold as a slave, immediately tell your master that he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is, and how to bring up his children.
source: Epictetus, Discourses 4.1.116 (Long; file edition 1890)
speaker: Epictetus, in conversation with an interlocutor
source_quote: when he was taken prisoner, how did he behave to the pirates? Did he call any of them master? ... How did he reprove them for feeding badly their captives? How was he sold? Did he seek a master? no; but a slave. And when he was sold how did he behave to his master? Immediately he disputed with him and said to his master that he ought not to be dressed as he was, nor shaved in such a manner; and about the children he told them how he ought to bring them up.
source_lesson: And so in every matter, it is absolutely necessary that he who has skill must be the superior of him who has not. Whoever then generally possesses the science of life, what else must he be than master?
source_verdict: And what was strange in this? for if his master had bought an exercise master, would he have employed him in the exercises of the palaestra as a servant or as a master?
source_missing: The vignette leaves out that he acted as one who possessed the science of life and was inwardly free. He never thought of himself as anyone's slave and, when sold, sought a slave rather than a master. This is why he could rightly instruct his buyer, as any skilled expert would.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats his capture and sale as externals that are neither good nor evil, and treats only his own purpose and his role as teacher as his business. 'Immediately' after being 'taken prisoner by pirates and sold as a slave' he does not lament, fear or flatter. Instead he goes on correcting how others live: he tells the master 'he ought not to be dressed or shaved as he is' and 'how to bring up his children'.
stoic_reason: Body, property and status are not up to us (Handbook 1). So slavery is material for his moral purpose, not an evil, and the scene shows no assented fear or grief about it (R2). He keeps to his role as a philosopher who advises others for their good (R6, Discourses 2.10). The most likely judgement behind the act is correct, though vanity or contrariness cannot be ruled out from one sentence (R1).

other: You see a Lacedaemonian, blinded in one eye by a young fellow-citizen the people turned over to him for whatever vengeance he desires, refrain, and bring him up and make a good man of him.
self: You, blinded in one eye by a young fellow-citizen the people turned over to you for whatever vengeance you desire, refrain, and bring him up and make a good man of him.
source: Epictetus, Fragment 5 (Oldfather, 1928; private seed)
speaker: Epictetus, as recorded by Rufus in notes on friendship
source_quote: this he refrained from doing, but brought him up and made a good man of him, and presented him in the theatre
source_verdict: What man among us does not admire the saying of Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian?
source_missing: The vignette leaves out Lycurgus's own stated reason, the saying the author admires. When the Lacedaemonians were surprised, he presented the man in the theatre and said he had received him insolent and violent and was returning him reasonable and public-spirited.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the loss of his eye, which is not up to him, as no real evil. He sees the young man's bad moral purpose as the true harm, and its correction as the good to be done. This is suggested by "refrain" (he declines the vengeance offered, "whatever vengeance he desires") and by his choosing instead to "bring him up and make a good man of him".
stoic_reason: The eye is an external, and the offender's greatest loss is his right moral purpose, so there is no ground for anger (Discourses 1.18; Handbook 20). Acting from that correct judgement, with an act that reason urges, is acting well (R1, R2 by contrast, R5).
also_in: Musonius Rufus, Lectures / Fragments (ancient; translator uncredited in 2015 anthology)

He declines to assent to the passion (R2, inverted) and answers the abuse calmly and wittily. That is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5), and fitting for a teacher of the school (R6).

source_quote: Marcus decided the attempted coup was an *opportunity.* They could, he said to his soldiers, go out and "settle this affair well and show to all mankind there is a right way to deal even with civil wars." It was a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship, to continue faithful to one who has broken faith." ... Marcus "was so greatly grieved at the death of Cassius that he could not bring himself even to look at the severed head of his enemy, but before the murderers drew near gave orders that it should be buried." He proceeded to treat each of Avidius's collaborators with leniency, including several senators who had actively endorsed this attempted coup. "I implore you, the senate, to keep my reign unstained by the blood of any senator," Marcus later appealed to those who wanted vengeance on his behalf. "May it never happen."
source_reason: It was a chance "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship, to continue faithful to one who has broken faith."
source_lesson: His dictum in life and in leadership was simple and straightforward: "Do the right thing. The rest doesn't matter."
source_verdict: Incredibly, Marcus decided the attempted coup was an *opportunity.* ... An assassin would soon enough take down Avidius, hoping almost certainly to impress himself to Marcus, and in the process revealing just how different a plane Marcus Aurelius was operating on.
stoic_judgement: He treats a wrong done to him as no harm to what is his own, so it gives no ground for anger or revenge. He treats keeping goodwill and forgiveness as the good he can achieve. This shows in his treating each collaborator with leniency and in his stated reason: "to forgive a man who has wronged one, to remain a friend to one who has transgressed friendship."
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from the judgement that the wrongdoer's fault harms only the wrongdoer and gives no ground for anger (Discourses 1.18; Handbook 20, 42), so it is well done (R1, R2). Clemency to those under his authority fits a ruler's role as guardian rather than enemy (R6), though the scene does not say how he weighed the state's safety, which leaves some doubt.
