source_quote: When the friends who were present at his execution wept over his fate, Seneca chastised them.
source_reason: What, he asked, had become of their Stoicism?
source_verdict: He never feels grief, since he realizes that grief is an “irrational contraction of the soul.”
stoic_judgement: He treats his own death, which is not up to him, as no evil, and treats his friends' weeping as a false judgement that it is one. That is why he recalls them to their principles. Shown by: "chastise the friends weeping over his fate", "asking what had become of their Stoicism", said at his own execution.
stoic_reason: He faces a condemnation that is not up to him without the judgement that death is dreadful (Handbook 5). He uses his moral purpose rightly, and his rebuke turns his friends from externals back to what is their own (Discourses 1.29, R1). Recalling friends to right judgement is a service to them, not the failure of sympathy that Handbook 16 warns the comforter against, since he is not here comforting a mourner (R4).
also_in: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)

other: You see a man whose neck is covered with wens and whose feet are diseased joking about his own deformities so much that others have nothing to add.
self: You, whose neck is covered with wens and whose feet are diseased, joke about your own deformities so much that others have nothing to add.
contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.55)
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Seneca's description of Vatinius
source_quote: joked about his own deformities so much that others had nothing to add
source_lesson: Of the kinds of humor we might use in response to an insult, self-deprecating humor can be particularly effective.
source_verdict: self-deprecating humor can be particularly effective
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats his body's defects, which are not up to him, as no evil and nothing to be ashamed of, and others' mockery as unable to harm him. The vignette shows this in 'joking about his own deformities so much that others have nothing to add.' A less likely reading: he jokes to get ahead of ridicule, still caring what others think of him.
stoic_reason: The body is not under our control (Handbook 1). It is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your judgement (Handbook 20). A man who freely laughs at his own wens shows he does not judge them evils, so the act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8). Some weight stays on the reading that he jokes to fend off scorn, which would treat reputation as a good he must protect (R2). Epictetus's caution against making it one's business to raise a laugh (Handbook 33) also counts slightly against him.

other: You see a Stoic judge, holding the power of the state, order that a Christian philosopher who refused to sacrifice to the gods be scourged and put to death, seeing a threat to public order and his power.
self: You, a Stoic judge holding the power of the state, order that a Christian philosopher who refused to sacrifice to the gods be scourged and put to death, seeing a threat to public order and your power.
source: Ryan Holiday & Stephen Hanselman, *Lives of the Stoics* (2020); source: The Acts of Justin
speaker: Holiday & Hanselman
source_quote: Holding the immense power of the state in his hands, Rusticus chose to use it. “Let those who have refused to sacrifice to the gods and to obey the command of the emperor,” he ordered, “be scourged and led away to suffer capital punishment according to the ruling of the laws.”
source_reason: All he saw was a threat to the public order, a threat to his power. ... Duty-bound, Rusticus had done what he believed he had needed to do.
source_lesson: We think we are doing the right thing. We think we are protecting the status quo. We do terrible things in the process.
source_verdict: It would be a stain on two otherwise flawless reputations. ... For the former's failure to see a bigger picture, he would be a villain to millions of Christians for the rest of history.
source_missing: Justin was a single, powerless dissenter whose example mattered very little and who could have been let go. Rusticus also acted partly out of personal frustration and contempt, taking Justin's remark that Romans 'hold fast in error' personally, rather than as a neutral enforcer of the law.
stoic_judgement: He treats keeping his own power, an external not up to him, as a good to defend, and the philosopher's refusal as an evil to stamp out by force. The vignette shows this in 'holding the power of the state' and 'seeing a threat to public order and his power'.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R2, an act that comes from the judgement that office and power are goods to be guarded is badly done, because such a man 'must end by subordinating himself to others' (Discourses 1.4) and acts from fear and craving. By R6, his role as judge could justify sentencing as 'a curator and guardian' for the law and the man's good, but here the stated motive includes his own power, and he punishes another man for a choice that lies within that man's own moral purpose.

other: You see a woman, three years after her son's death, as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him, spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by his death.
self: You, three years after your son's death, are as grief-stricken as on the day you buried him, spending your days thinking bitterly about the happiness you have been deprived of by his death.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, relaying Seneca's consolation and advice to Marcia
source_quote: a woman who, three years after the death of her son, was as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him... spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by the death of her son
source_lesson: By engaging in retrospective negative visualization, Seneca thinks, we can replace our feelings of regret at having lost something with feelings of thanks for once having had it.
source_verdict: Rather than spending her days thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by the death of her son, Marcia should, says Seneca, think about how much worse off she would be today if she had never been able to enjoy his company.
stoic_judgement: She treats her son's life, which is not up to her, as the good her happiness depended on, and his death as an evil that has robbed her of it. The vignette shows this in "thinking bitterly about the happiness she has been deprived of by his death" and in her being, three years on, "as grief-stricken as on the day she buried him."
stoic_reason: It is not the death that distresses her but her judgement about it (Handbook 5). She has assented to the passion of grief by judging an external loss to be an evil that took her good (R2, R4: judging the loss an evil is the fault). This is sustained, deliberate brooding, not unwilled tears at the first blow, so R3 does not apply. She also does not take the death 'as a thing returned' (Handbook 11) but goes on desiring what is not under her control.
also_in: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)

other: You see a Roman statesman go out in public without shoes or tunic, to accustom himself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things.
self: You, a Roman statesman, go out in public without shoes or tunic, to accustom yourself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Plutarch on Cato
source_quote: Cato made a point of ignoring the dictates of fashion: When everyone was wearing light purple, he wore dark, and although ancient Romans normally went out in public wearing shoes and a tunic, Cato wore neither.
source_reason: not because he "sought vainglory"; to the contrary, he dressed differently in order to accustom himself "to be ashamed only of what was really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things."
source_lesson: In other words, Cato consciously did things to trigger the disdain of other people simply so he could practice ignoring their disdain.
source_verdict: Another way to overcome our obsession with winning the admiration of other people is to go out of our way to do things likely to trigger their disdain.
stoic_judgement: He treats only what is truly shameful as shameful, and others' low opinion of indifferent things such as dress as nothing to him. The vignette states this: "to accustom himself to be ashamed only of what is really shameful, and to ignore men's low opinion of other things."
stoic_reason: Reputation is not up to us (Handbook 1). He is deliberately training his judgement so that it no longer treats others' opinion as a good or an evil, which is progress as Discourses 1.4 describes it. His stated motive is correct, so the act is well done (R1, R5). The training is aimed at freeing himself from opinion, not at display, so it does not fall foul of Epictetus's warnings against showy exercises. Some small doubt remains about whether this suits a statesman's role (R6).

other: You see an academic, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, answer a colleague who is trying to decide whether to characterize him in print as evil or merely misguided: "Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?"
self: You, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, answer a colleague who is trying to decide whether to characterize you in print as evil or merely misguided: "Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?"
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine
source_quote: having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, I had the presence of mind to respond to this insult in a Stoically acceptable manner, with self-deprecating humor: “Why can’t you portray me as being both evil and misguided?” I asked.
source_lesson: Self-deprecating humor has become my standard response to insults.
source_verdict: But on that particular day, having fallen under the influence of the Stoics, I had the presence of mind to respond to this insult in a Stoically acceptable manner, with self-deprecating humor
stoic_judgement: He treats his reputation, how a colleague portrays him in print, as not up to him and so neither good nor evil. He also treats being evil and being misguided as one thing, since for the Stoics wrongdoing comes from wrong judgement. The evidence is the vignette's 'having fallen under the influence of the Stoics' and his calm reply inviting the harsher portrayal: 'Why can't you portray me as being both evil and misguided?'
stoic_reason: Reputation is among the things 'not under our control' (Handbook 1). He does not take the colleague's verdict as an insult (Handbook 20) or as an evil to fend off. This follows Epictetus's advice to answer evil-speaking by granting even more faults instead of defending oneself (Handbook 33). By R1, the act proceeds from a correct judgement, so it is well done for a person making progress (R5); the small chance of flippancy or hidden vanity keeps some weight on the other readings.
also_in: Massimo Pigliucci, How to Be a Stoic (2017)

other: You see a man, left sitting nearly an hour in a doctor's waiting room because the doctor is woefully behind schedule, find it impossible to get angry because he is thinking about anger during that hour.
self: You are left sitting nearly an hour in a doctor's waiting room because the doctor is woefully behind schedule, and you find it impossible to get angry because you are thinking about anger during that hour.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, narrating his own experience as a practicing Stoic
source_quote: I found it impossible to get angry.
source_reason: because I was thinking about anger during that hour
source_lesson: But one thing I have found is that the more you think about and understand anger, the easier it is to control it.
source_verdict: But one thing I have found is that the more you think about and understand anger, the easier it is to control it.
source_missing: He was thinking about anger because he was reading Seneca's essay on anger while he waited, as a practicing Stoic working to understand and control his anger.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the delay as no real harm. Spending the hour 'thinking about anger' suggests he is examining the passion and so withholds assent from the impression that the doctor's lateness wrongs him: 'find it impossible to get angry because he is thinking about anger during that hour'.
stoic_reason: It is not the doctor's lateness that would insult him but his judgement that it does (Handbook 20). The doctor's schedule is not up to him; his use of impressions is (Handbook 1). Using the hour to study anger instead of assenting to it reads as a man making progress who puts his principles into practice (Discourses 1.4), so R1, R2 (by contrast) and R5 give 'well'. There is some weight on 'neither' because the absence of anger might be mere absorption rather than a corrected judgement (R7).

other: You see a man, exiled after he or his father adulterated Sinope's coinage, respond to someone shaming him that the people of Sinope sentenced him to exile, but he sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
self: When someone brings up how you or your father adulterated Sinope's coinage, to shame you, you respond that the people of Sinope sentenced you to exile, but you sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, citing Musonius
source_quote: when someone later brought up this incident in an attempt to shame him, Diogenes, with typical Cynic wit, responded that although it was true that the people of Sinope had sentenced him to exile, he in turn had sentenced them to remain in Sinope.
source_lesson: Musonius also reminds us that exile has changed people for the better. ... It has also transformed ordinary people, such as Diogenes of Sinope, into philosophers.
source_verdict: Diogenes, with typical Cynic wit, responded
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats exile, and the shaming that goes with it, as no evil: place and reputation are not up to him, and the citizens' verdict does not touch his moral purpose. The words that suggest it: he answers the shaming by turning the sentence around ('he sentenced them to remain in Sinope'), so he shows no felt disgrace at losing his city.
stoic_reason: By Handbook 20, the insult lies only in one's judgement that one is insulted. By Handbook 1, exile and reputation are not under our control. He refuses that judgement and treats exile as an indifferent, which is acting well (R1, R2 by contrast). A less likely reading is that the retort is wounded vanity striking back, and the scene leaves this open (R1).

self: You, experimenting with a simplified lifestyle, are asked where you got the T-shirt you are wearing, answer that you bought it at a thrift store, and find yourself feeling a bit ashamed.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it: Epictetus's framing does not settle whether 'find himself feeling a bit ashamed' shows assent to the judgement that low status is an evil (vice, R2) or only an involuntary first movement (neutral, R3). The honest answer also pulls toward 'well'. No reading is clearly most likely. | no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.45) | The source's author judges it neither; Epictetus's framing gives vice
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own experience
source_quote: When, for example, someone asked me where I had gotten the T-shirt I was wearing and I answered that I had bought it at a thrift store, I found myself feeling a bit ashamed.
source_lesson: He wanted to teach himself "to be ashamed only of what was really shameful."
source_verdict: He therefore went out of his way to do things that would trigger inappropriate feelings of shame in himself, simply so he could practice overcoming such feelings. I have lately been trying to emulate Cato in this respect.
stoic_judgement: He answers truthfully ('he bought it at a thrift store'), so he does not treat lying about his status as acceptable. But 'find himself feeling a bit ashamed' suggests a judgement that being seen as poor or low-status, a matter of reputation outside his control, is something bad. Alternatively, 'find himself' may mark only an unwilled flicker that he does not assent to.
stoic_reason: Reputation is not up to us (Handbook 1). Shame at being thought cheap is the singer's wanting applause (Discourses 2.13), a passion if assented to (R2). If it is only a sudden unconsidered movement, it is not a fault (fragment 9, R3). The honest answer itself is an appropriate act, but the scene's focus is the shame.

other: You see a Roman emperor whose citizens tell jokes at his expense, and he does not punish them for doing so.
self: You are a Roman emperor, and when citizens tell jokes at your expense, you do not punish them for doing so.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: Irvine, recounting the life and reign of the emperor Marcus Aurelius
source_quote: Citizens told jokes at his expense and were not punished for doing so.
source_lesson: It is therefore with good reason that Marcus observed, in his Meditations, that "the art of living is more like wrestling than dancing."
source_verdict: As Roman emperors go, Marcus was exceptionally good. For one thing, he exercised great restraint in his use of power.
stoic_judgement: Most likely he treats the jokes as no harm to him. His reputation is not up to him, and being mocked is not an evil, so he does not judge himself insulted and gives no anger room. The vignette suggests this when it says his citizens 'tell jokes at his expense, and he does not punish them for doing so', even though his office gives him the power to punish.
stoic_reason: Handbook 20 says it is our own judgement, not the one who reviles us, that insults us. An emperor who could punish mockery and does not most plausibly holds that reputation is outside his control (Handbook 1) and shows his subjects what is due to them in his role (R1, R2 by contrast, R6). The scene does not exclude a worse motive, such as forbearing only to win popularity (R1).

other: You see a Stoic who took up competitive rowing working through his fears of flipping, of rowing in the predawn darkness, and of being out in a tiny boat hundreds of yards from shore, choosing activities that give him butterflies simply so he can practice dealing with them.
self: You, having taken up competitive rowing as a Stoic, work through your fears of flipping, of rowing in the predawn darkness, and of being out in a tiny boat hundreds of yards from shore, choosing activities that give you butterflies simply so you can practice dealing with them.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own practice of Stoicism
source_quote: It took me considerable effort to overcome my fear of flipping \(by successfully surviving three flips\). From there, I went on to work through other fears, including a fear of rowing in the predawn darkness, a fear of pushing off from the dock while standing up in the boat, and a fear of being out in the middle of a lake, hundreds of yards from the nearest shore, in a tiny boat \(that has thrice betrayed me\).
source_reason: I like to engage in activities, such as competitive rowing, that give me butterflies simply so I can practice dealing with them.
source_lesson: These feelings are, after all, an important component of the fear of failure, so that by dealing with them I am working to overcome my fear of failure.
source_verdict: I like to engage in activities, such as competitive rowing, that give me butterflies simply so I can practice dealing with them.
stoic_judgement: He treats his fear of flipping, of the dark and of open water as something to train out through practice, not as a sign that these externals are real evils. He treats the work on his own response as the thing that matters. The text shows this in 'working through his fears' and 'choosing activities that give him butterflies simply so he can practice dealing with them'.
stoic_reason: He puts himself in front of frightening impressions on purpose so he can practise assenting correctly to them, which is the training in desire and aversion that Epictetus calls most pressing (Discourses 3.2) and the daily practice of a man making progress (Discourses 1.4). The 'butterflies' read as first movements, not assented dread (fragment 9, R3), and the deliberate choice to train shows a correct judgement behind the act (R1, R5).

other: You see a man feeling a bit depressed taking a trip to cheer himself up, thinking a change of scenery might help to improve his mood.
self: You are feeling a bit depressed and take a trip to cheer yourself up, thinking a change of scenery might help to improve your mood.
contested_note: no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.50)
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
chapter: Wherever You Go, There You Are: You Can't Escape Yourself
speaker: David Fideler, recounting Seneca's comment to Lucilius
source_quote: LUCILIUS WAS FEELING A BIT DEPRESSED and wanted to cheer himself up by taking a trip, as many people do today.
source_reason: He thought a change of scenery might help to improve his mood.
source_lesson: But as Seneca commented, "You must change the mind, not the location," because "your faults will travel with you wherever you go."
source_verdict: Unfortunately, the project was a failure: Lucilius's depression was not cured.
stoic_judgement: He treats his low mood as something an external, a different place, can fix: 'taking a trip to cheer himself up, thinking a change of scenery might help to improve his mood.' Feeling 'a bit depressed' suggests he has accepted some distress, though its cause is not given.
stoic_reason: For Epictetus, men are disturbed not by things but by their judgements about them (Handbook 5). So the man most likely has a passion of distress and looks for its cure in something not up to him, the scenery, rather than in correcting his own judgements. That reading makes his act proceed from a mistaken judgement (R1, R2). The trip itself is an indifferent type of act, and a mild low mood could be only a first movement, so 'neither' keeps real weight (R3, R7).

other: You see a novice banjo player, asked by his teacher to play in the students' recital, agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause himself psychological discomfort and to confront his fear of failing.
self: You, a novice banjo player asked by your teacher to play in the students' recital, agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause yourself psychological discomfort and to confront your fear of failing.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, narrating his own experience as a Stoic practitioner
source_quote: I initially rejected the offer; it sounded like no fun at all to risk public humiliation trying to play banjo in front of a bunch of strangers. But then it occurred to me that this was a wonderful opportunity to cause myself psychological discomfort and to confront—and hopefully vanquish—my fear of failing. I agreed to take part.
source_reason: this was a wonderful opportunity to cause myself psychological discomfort and to confront—and hopefully vanquish—my fear of failing.
source_lesson: By taking part in the recital, in other words, I immunized myself against a fair amount of future anxiety.
source_verdict: Not at all. In causing myself anxiety by, for example, giving a banjo recital, I have precluded much future anxiety in my life.
stoic_judgement: He treats his fear of failing as a fault in his own judgement that he should work on, and treats the recital's outcome (a good performance, applause, not failing) as something not worth fearing. The words: "agree to take part because it is a wonderful opportunity to cause himself psychological discomfort and to confront his fear of failing".
stoic_reason: He uses an external, the recital, as material for his moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). He trains the first field, aversion, against the singer's anxiety over what is not up to him (Discourses 2.13, 3.2), and in doing so accepts his teacher's request as a student should (R6). This is acting well as one making progress (R1, R2, R5).

other: You see a father whose little son has just fallen down the steep stairs and scraped his back respond calmly, with concern but without panic, feeling no shock or surprise because he had anticipated it.
self: When your little son falls down the steep stairs and scrapes his back, you respond calmly, with concern but without panic, feeling no shock or surprise because you had anticipated it.
source: David Fideler, Breakfast with Seneca (2022; original translations by Fideler, with Elizabeth Mercier)
speaker: David Fideler, the author, recounting his own experience with his son Benjamin
source_quote: Since this was a serious concern, I would imagine Benjamin falling down the stairs and hurting himself. That way, if it actually happened, at least I'd be fully prepared for it. ... The Stoic training I had used allowed me to respond to the misfortune calmly—with concern, but without panic.
source_reason: There was no sense of shock or surprise when it happened, because I had anticipated it.
source_lesson: Rehearsing a potential disaster in advance increases your ability to cope and think clearly should the imagined disaster ever take place.
source_verdict: While this sounds like a slightly unpleasant exercise, I'm glad I did it
source_missing: The vignette leaves out that the father had deliberately and repeatedly rehearsed, in his imagination, his son falling down the stairs and how he would respond depending on how badly the boy was hurt (the Stoic praemeditatio malorum). It also omits that he had first taken every physical precaution he could: a railing, a locked gate and friction tape on the stairs.
stoic_judgement: The father treats his son's fall and scrape as something that happens to a mortal child and is not an evil, and treats caring for the boy as what is up to him and what his role asks. The words that show it: 'respond calmly, with concern but without panic', and 'no shock or surprise because he had anticipated it'.
stoic_reason: He has not assented to the impression that an external (the child's body) has suffered an evil, so no passion of fear or grief arises (R2, Handbook 5). His concern is affection joined with reason, which Discourses 1.11 calls 'right and good' (R4), and caring for the boy is what the father's role asks (R6, Discourses 2.10). So he acts well as one making progress (R5).

speaker: David Fideler, the author, recounting his wealthy next-door neighbor Fred as an example of Seneca's point
source_quote: Once, when I experienced a personal tragedy, Fred walked over to my house to see how I was doing. When we talked, he said, "When something like that happens, I think you can only put it in God's hands."
source_lesson: In any case, Fred is a perfect example of what Seneca had in mind when saying that if you possess wealth, you have a fabulous opportunity to practice virtue.
source_verdict: he was also down-to-earth, easy to talk with, and never once showed the least bit of arrogance or extravagance
stoic_judgement: He treats his neighbour's welfare as worth attending to, and the tragedy as something outside human control, to be accepted rather than fought: he walks over "to see how he is doing" and says "you can only put it in God's hands."
stoic_reason: Visiting a grieving neighbour is an appropriate act of the neighbour's role (Discourses 2.10). Sympathy in words is right (Handbook 16), and his counsel points the neighbour to what is not up to him and to providence (Handbook 1), so the act most likely proceeds from correct judgements (R1, R4, R6). A small chance remains that the words are a dismissive platitude.

speaker: David Fideler, the author, telling a story from his own life
source_quote: I decided to go on the trip, which was unforgettable. But when I was alone in my room, I sometimes broke down into tears, because of the grief and disappointment that had followed me there.

The vignette calls him 'grieving a recent breakup', and he 'break[s] down in tears alone in his room' days after the loss, not at the first blow. His choice to go to the villa ('a once-in-a-lifetime chance and costs almost nothing') looks like a reasonable choice of a preferred indifferent and shows no fault.

Grief assented to, the judgement that losing an external is an evil, is acting badly even with no outward deed (R2). Tears alone do not decide the label (R4): they might be an unwilled first movement (R3). But 'grieving' and 'break down' point more to assent than to a passing shock.

other: You see a son who, after enduring his stroke-weakened mother's pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink, asks the nurse and, on her advice, pops an ice cube into his mother's mouth.
self: You, after enduring your stroke-weakened mother's pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink, ask the nurse and, on her advice, pop an ice cube into your mother's mouth.
source: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)
speaker: William B. Irvine, the author, recounting his own experience caring for his mother
source_quote: I became my mother’s personal ice man, bringing a cup on each visit. ... I would pop a cube into her mouth, and she would, while sucking it, tell me how wonderful the ice was.

source_verdict: Watching her suck appreciatively on ice cubes, I felt a tinge of envy. Wouldn’t it be wonderful, I thought, to be able to derive this much pleasure from a simple ice cube?

The words that show this: he is 'enduring' her 'pleas for a glass of water she cannot safely drink', yet he does not give it. He 'asks the nurse' and acts 'on her advice', giving 'an ice cube' instead.

This fits the man making progress who "when he rises in the morning ... proceeds to keep and observe" his principles (Discourses 1.4), and Epictetus's advice to keep death daily before one's eyes. Some weight goes to 'neither' because the scene shows only the question, not what he does with the answer, and 'would I want' could track desire rather than what is appropriate (R5, R7).

Wanting to stay for pleasure, against that duty, reads as an assented desire for externals that are not up to him, which is acting badly even before any outward deed (Handbook 1; Discourses 3.2; R1, R2). Nothing in the scene suggests a first movement or an act reason neither urges nor forbids, so there is little ground for neutral (R7).

stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the security of his throne, or the punishment of a usurper's whole line, as a good great enough to override his father's pardon and the good faith it pledged. Even if he sincerely thinks them traitors, the one deceived is he himself (Handbook 42). His roles call for something else: as son he should honour his father's orders, and as ruler he should punish as a guardian, not as an enemy (R6; Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10), so this is acting badly.

For this would be the one profit I could gain from my present troubles, if I were able to bring the matter to an honorable conclusion, and show all the world that there is a right way to deal even with civil war.

He reasoned that Cassius, one of his most esteemed and trusted generals, had acted from ignorance (no man does wrong knowingly), and he regarded the rebels as kin to be treated as a physician treats patients, not as enemies.
stoic_judgement: He treats a right way of acting, even toward those who rose against him, as the good to be shown. He does not treat revenge or his own injury as what matters. The words that show this: "pardon his rebel general, a usurper, and all ranged against him, to show all the world there is a right way to deal even with civil war."
stoic_reason: As ruler he acts from his role (R6). He does not judge the rebellion, which is outside his control, to be a harm that calls for anger, since the rebels' error is their own loss (Discourses 1.18; Handbook 42). The stated reason points to a correct judgement, so the act is well done (R1, R5). A smaller probability goes to the reading that he wants reputation, the applause that is not up to us (Discourses 2.13).

Any wince at the fall itself would be only a first movement (R3). His assent shows no passion, so he acts well as one making progress (R5).

stoic_reason: The act comes from a correct judgement: anger is a faulty judgement and is not to be acted on. That is acting well for a person making progress who withholds assent to the impulse (R1, R5; Discourses 1.18, Handbook 20). Some weight goes to 'badly' because the scene says he is angry, and an assented passion is acting badly even without an outward deed (R2). Little weight goes to 'neither', since this is more than a first movement (R3).

The vignette shows this in 'drink undismayed' and 'because he feels more confidence in his friend', and the warning was strong, since it came from his mother.
stoic_reason: Death is nothing dreadful; the judgement that it is dreadful is (Handbook 5). His act proceeds from a judgement that a friend's good faith is to be honoured over fear for the body, a correct judgement in his role as friend and patient (R1, R6). He does not assent to dread (R2), and he acts on the preferred indifferent, health, with reason (Discourses 2.10).

speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger, writing to Novatus
source_quote: In his anger he ordered a soldier to be led off to execution because he had returned from furlough without his comrade, as though he must have murdered him if he could not show him. ... Piso even added a third: for he actually ordered the centurion, who had brought back the condemned man, to be put to death.
source_reason: “You,” it says, “I order to be executed, because you have been condemned to death: you, because you have been the cause of your comrade’s condemnation, and you, because when ordered to put him to death you disobeyed your general.”
source_lesson: O, how clever is anger at inventing reasons for its frenzy\!
source_verdict: What could be more unworthy than this? Because one was proved to be innocent, two perished.
source_missing: The vignette leaves out that Piso gave the order in a fury. It also omits that the original condemnation rested only on the soldier returning without his comrade, and that Piso refused him time to search. The stated reasons were invented because no real crime could be found.
stoic_judgement: The general most likely treats the standing of his own verdict and command, an external thing (reputation, office), as a good to protect over the lives of men he now knows are innocent of murder. The vignette shows this: he orders the execution even though 'the comrade [is] alive', and his three reasons, 'for being condemned, for causing the condemnation, for disobeying his general', are about his sentence and authority, not about any crime that happened.
stoic_reason: The act comes from the bad judgement that preserving his decree is worth more than justice. Killing a man for having been wrongly condemned is an act reason forbids (R1, R2; Discourses 4.8: 'that which proceeds from bad judgements is badly done'). A general's role asks for discipline, but not the death of the innocent (R6), so the role does not excuse it.

source_lesson: While you are angry, you ought not to be allowed to do anything.
source_verdict: Can anyone wish to grant the power of revenge to an angry man, when Plato himself gave up his own right to exercise it?
stoic_judgement: He treats his own angry impulse as untrustworthy and the slave's due correction, not an excess beyond it, as what should be done. The vignette shows this in "because in his rage he would beat him more than he ought" and in his handing the punishment to his associate. He also plainly holds the angry judgement that the slave's fault has harmed him ("rather angry", "in his rage").
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a correct judgement: he refuses to act on his anger and keeps the punishment to what is due (R1, R6, Handbook 20). But the anger itself is a passion already assented to, not a first movement, so in feeling he is acting badly (R2; Discourses 1.18). He reads as a man making progress who restrains an assented passion (R5), so 'well' is only slightly more likely than 'badly'.

other: You see a philosopher who, when he is given a box on the ear by a man, merely says that it is a pity a man cannot tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking.
self: You, when you are given a box on the ear by a man, merely say that it is a pity a man cannot tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.11 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, advising the reader how to check anger
source_quote: when he was given a box on the ear, merely said that it was a pity a man could not tell when he ought to wear his helmet out walking
source_lesson: It does not so much matter how an injury is done, as how it is borne; and I do not see how moderation can be hard to practise, when I know that even despots, though success and impunity combine to swell their pride, have sometimes restrained their natural ferocity.
source_verdict: It does not so much matter how an injury is done, as how it is borne; and I do not see how moderation can be hard to practise, when I know that even despots, though success and impunity combine to swell their pride, have sometimes restrained their natural ferocity.
stoic_judgement: He treats the blow as no evil to himself and not as an insult, since it touches only his body, which is not up to him. The words that suggest it: he "merely says" a mild jest about wearing a helmet, with no retaliation, complaint or show of injury.
stoic_reason: It is not the man who strikes you who insults you but your judgement that he does (Handbook 20), and the body is not under our control (Handbook 1). Reading his calm, light reply as coming from that correct judgement, he acts well (R1, R2 by contrast), keeping his anger in check and enduring the abuse.
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.32 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, citing Cato
source_quote: Afterwards when he was apologizing, Cato replied, "I do not remember being struck."
source_reason: He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
source_lesson: It is the part of a great mind to despise wrongs done to it; the most contemptuous form of revenge is not to deem one's adversary worth taking vengeance upon.
source_verdict: He thought it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it.
stoic_judgement: He treats revenge as no good and the blow as no real harm to him. The vignette states this directly: 'thinking it better to ignore the insult than to revenge it'. His reply, 'I do not remember being struck', shows that he refuses to keep the blow before his mind or count it against the man.
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from a correct judgement (R1). It is not the striker who insults you but your judgement that he does (Handbook 20), and there is no ground for anger at a man (Discourses 1.18). Not assenting to anger and declining revenge is acting well as one making progress (R2, R5).
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see a distinguished Roman knight, whose son the emperor has just had executed, dine at the emperor's banquet with a countenance which betrays no ill will, shedding no tear, because he has another son.
self: You, a distinguished Roman knight whose son the emperor has just had executed, dine at the emperor's banquet with a countenance which betrays no ill will, shedding no tear, because you have another son.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it: Epictetus's framing turns on whether the restraint comes from caution and a father's duty or from fear, and the scene supports both. 'Because he has another son' could also mean he grieves little because a son remains, which would be a third reading. | no reading clearly most likely (top probability 0.55)
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.33 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: Pastor came with a countenance which betrayed no ill will. ... he shed no tear the while; he did not permit his grief to betray itself by the slightest sign; he dined just as though his entreaties had gained his son's life.
source_reason: he had another son. ... he would have lost his second son had he proved an unacceptable guest to the murderer of his eldest.
source_lesson: It is often so far from expedient to avenge our wrongs, that it will not do even to admit them.
source_verdict: The wrongs of the powerful must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the safety of his remaining son as what his role as a father now asks him to protect. That outweighs any display of grief or resentment toward the emperor. The words 'because he has another son' give his reason; 'betrays no ill will, shedding no tear' show the restraint it produces.
stoic_reason: His son's death and the emperor's power are not up to him; his conduct at the table is (Handbook 1). Read as a father caring for his living son with rational caution, an eupatheia, and acting for a preferred indifferent, this is acting well in his role (R1, R4, R6, Discourses 2.10). Read as fear that the emperor will take this son too, judging an external loss an evil, it is an assented passion and so acting badly (R2, Discourses 2.13).

self: You see a man digging and vigorously brandishing a mattock, complain that the sight makes you weary, and forbid him to work where you can see him.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.25 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: complained that the sight made him weary, and forbade the man to work where he could see him. The same man complained that he had suffered from the rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double.
source_reason: the sight made him weary ... he had suffered from the rose-leaves upon which he lay being folded double
source_lesson: Nothing, therefore, nourishes anger more than excessive and dissatisfied luxury: the mind ought to be hardened by rough treatment, so as not to feel any blow that is not severe.
source_verdict: When pleasures have corrupted both the body and the mind, nothing seems endurable, not indeed because it is hard, but because he who has to bear it is soft
stoic_judgement: He treats his own ease, being spared even the sight of toil, as a good, and the sight of another man working as an evil done to him. He also treats the man's work as something to be removed for his comfort. The vignette shows this in 'complain that the sight makes him weary' and 'forbid the man to work where he can see him'.
stoic_reason: It is not the digging that wearies him but his judgement about it (Handbook 5). He assents to an aversion toward something not up to him and acts on it by hindering another man's lawful work. This is an assented passion carried into a deed (R2, R1). It is no mere first movement (R3), since he complains and gives an order.

other: You see a king's closest friend, who had advised him to drink more sparingly, look at his son shot through the heart by the drunken king and reply that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
self: You, the king's closest friend who advised him to drink more sparingly, look at your son shot through the heart by the drunken king and reply that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, telling the story as an example that anger can be suppressed
source_quote: He replied, that Apollo himself could not have taken better aim.
source_reason: He thought that the breast of his son being torn asunder, and his heart quivering with its wound, gave him an opportunity of making a complimentary speech.
source_lesson: the matter which we are now discussing, has been proved, I mean, that anger can be suppressed.
source_verdict: He actually praised an act which he ought not to have endured to witness. ... it was worse to praise that arrow-shot than to shoot it.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats staying in the king's favour, and his own safety, as goods he must keep, and the king's anger as an evil he must avoid. So he praises the murder of his own son as a fine shot. The vignette shows this in two places. He had earlier given the frank counsel 'to drink more sparingly'. Now, facing 'his son shot through the heart by the drunken king', he replies that 'Apollo himself could not have taken better aim'.
stoic_reason: The scene shows no unwilled first movement (R3). It shows a considered spoken act, and the most likely judgement behind it is fear: that what is not up to us (life, the king's favour) is good or evil (R1, R2; Discourses 2.13). That fear makes him lie and flatter (Handbook 52). It also betrays what his roles as father and as counsellor ask of him, which is truth and loyalty to his son, not praise of the killer (R6). Calmness in the face of the loss would not be the fault, but the scene gives no sign that his words come from that rather than from fear (R4).

other: You see a conqueror, never violent in anger, burn letters to his civil-war rival from men thought neutral or hostile, to put it out of his power to be angry, thinking the kindest pardon was not knowing their offence.
self: You, a conqueror never violent in anger, burn letters to your civil-war rival from men thought neutral or hostile, to put it out of your power to be angry, thinking the kindest pardon is not knowing their offence.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 2.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Anger
source_quote: he burned a packet of letters addressed to Gnaeus Pompeius by persons who had been thought to be either neutrals or on the other side.
source_reason: he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what his offence had been.
source_lesson: but the rarer moderation is among kings, the more it deserves to be praised.
source_verdict: Though he was never violent in his anger, yet he preferred to put it out of his power to be angry: he thought that the kindest way to pardon each of them was not to know what his offence had been.
stoic_judgement: He treats his own anger as the danger and pardon as the good. He also counts himself liable to anger, so he removes the impression before it can be assented to. The vignette shows this in "to put it out of his power to be angry" and "thinking the kindest pardon was not knowing their offence". "Never violent in anger" suggests a settled habit of restraint, not suppressed rage.
stoic_reason: R1, R2, R5 and R8 apply. The act proceeds from the correct judgement that what others did is not his to be harmed by, and that anger would be his own fault (Handbook 20; Discourses 1.18). Shielding himself from an impression he might wrongly assent to is the caution of a man making progress, and it serves kindness to the men whose fate lies in his hands. It is acting well in his role as victor.

self: You, a king hearing your soldiers curse you for bringing them into impassable mud, extricate the worst-stuck without their knowing their helper, and say, "Now curse the king, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.22 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: He also on one night, hearing some of his soldiers invoking everything that was evil upon their king for having brought them along that road and into that impassable mud, went to those who were in the greatest difficulties, and having extricated them without their knowing who was their helper, said, "Now curse Antigonus, by whose fault you have fallen into this trouble, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough."
source_lesson: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
source_verdict: what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
stoic_judgement: He treats the soldiers' cursing as no injury to him and treats their rescue, which falls to him as their commander, as what matters. This is shown by 'hearing his soldiers curse him', followed by his choice to 'extricate the worst-stuck without their knowing their helper', and by his mild, joking reply, 'Now curse the king, but bless the man who has brought you out of this slough.'
stoic_reason: It is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your judgement that he does (Handbook 20). The king forms no such judgement and answers abuse with help, not anger. He does what his role as king and leader of these men suggests (Handbook 30, Discourses 2.10), so the act proceeds from a correct judgement and is well done (R1, R6). Help given without seeking thanks shows kindness and the restraint of anger and vanity (R8).

source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.21 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: he swore to reduce the river which had carried off his royal retinue to so low an ebb that even women should walk across it and trample upon it. He thereupon devoted all the resources of his army to this object, and remained working until by cutting one hundred and eighty channels across the bed of the river he divided it into three hundred and sixty brooks, and left the bed dry, the waters flowing through other channels.
source_reason: one of the white horses which drew the royal chariot was washed away, and his loss moved the king to such violent rage
source_lesson: Thus he lost time, which is very important in great operations, and lost, also, the soldiers’ courage, which was broken by useless labour, and the opportunity of falling upon his enemy unprepared, while he was waging against the river the war which he had declared against his foes.
source_verdict: This frenzy, for what else can you call it, has befallen Romans also
stoic_judgement: He treats the loss of the white horse, an external not up to him, as an evil and an insult, and the river as something to punish. The vignette shows this in "enraged that a river washed away one of his chariot's white horses" and in his diverting "all his army's resources" to drying its bed while "hurrying to besiege Babylon."
stoic_reason: The rage is stated, and the whole army acts on it: this is an assented passion, not a first movement (R2, against R3). It comes from judging an external loss an evil (Handbook 5; Handbook 20, where it is our judgement that insults us), and his role as a king leading a campaign does not ask for vengeance on a river (R6).

self: You are a poor pupil whose fellow pupils each give your teacher large presents; finding nothing to give him which is worthy of him, you present him with the only thing you possess, yourself.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 1.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise on benefits
source_quote: Therefore I present you with the only thing I possess, myself.
source_reason: I can find nothing to give you which is worthy of you; I feel my poverty in this respect alone.
source_lesson: We must not consider how great presents are, but in what spirit they are given.
source_verdict: By this present Aeschines outdid Alcibiades, whose mind was as great as his Wealth, and all the splendour of the most wealthy youths of Athens.
stoic_judgement: He treats himself, his own moral purpose and devotion, as the one thing truly his and worth giving. He does not treat costly externals as the measure of a gift. Nor does he treat his poverty as an evil to be ashamed of beside the 'large presents' of his fellows. The words that suggest this: 'say he can find nothing worthy of him, and so present him with the only thing he possesses, himself.'
stoic_reason: He gives what is under his control (his own choice and self) and does not envy or compete in externals (Handbook 1, 19). As a pupil he renders what is due to his teacher (Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10). Read from the scene, the act most likely proceeds from a correct judgement (R1, R6).

self: You are a king, and hearing two common soldiers leaning against your tent speak evil of you, you gently raise the cloth and say, "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.22 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: Antigonus heard all they said, as was likely, since there was only a piece of cloth between the speakers and the listener, who gently raised it, .and said "Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you."
source_lesson: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
source_verdict: what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves
stoic_judgement: The king most likely judges that the soldiers' evil words do him no harm and give no ground for anger, and that what is up to him is a mild, kindly response, not revenge. The vignette shows this in: 'gently raise the cloth' and his good-humoured warning, 'Go a little further off, for fear the king should hear you'. He answers with restraint and even shields them, though as king he could punish.
stoic_reason: The insult lies in one's judgement, not in the speaker (Handbook 20). The reviler speaks from what seems good to him, so there is no ground for anger (Handbook 42; Discourses 1.18). The king's gentle act shows he did not assent to the impression of injury, and in his role as ruler he deals kindly with his men (R1, R2, R6).

self: When a demagogue spits upon your forehead while you are pleading a case, you wipe your face and say, "I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.38 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in an essay addressed to Novatus
source_quote: Cato wiped his face, and said, "Lentulus, I shall declare to all the world that men are mistaken when they say that you are wanting in cheek."
source_verdict: Yet how much better did our Cato behave?
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the spitting as no harm to himself: what is up to him is his own response, not the demagogue's act. He wipes his face and answers with a calm jest. The jest turns the act back on its doer as proof of the man's impudence ('wanting in cheek'). He does not strike back or break off his case, which suggests he did not assent to the impression that he has been injured.
stoic_reason: By Handbook 20 it is not the one who strikes or spits who insults you but your judgement that you are insulted. His composed, witty reply, with no retaliation, reads as a refusal of that judgement, so it is acting well as one making progress (R1, R2, R5). The retort could instead be read as a barb from wounded pride, so that reading keeps some probability.
also_in: William B. Irvine, A Guide to the Good Life (2009)

other: You see an emperor, shocked that his friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet, order the slave let go, the crystal broken, and the tank filled.
self: You, an emperor shocked that your friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet, order the slave let go, the crystal broken, and the tank filled.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.40 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Novatus
source_quote: Caesar was shocked at this novel form of cruelty, and ordered him to be let go, and, in his place, all the crystal ware which he saw before him to be broken, and the tank to be filled up.
source_reason: Caesar was shocked at this novel form of cruelty
source_lesson: This was the proper way for Caesar to reprove his friend: he made a good use of his power.
source_verdict: he made a good use of his power.
stoic_judgement: He treats a man's life as worth far more than a crystal goblet, and cruelty to the slave as the real wrong, not the loss of property. This is shown by 'shocked that his friend and host ordered a slave thrown to his fish for breaking a crystal goblet' and his orders: 'the slave let go, the crystal broken, and the tank filled'. Breaking the rest of the crystal and filling the tank suggest he judges these externals worthless next to the man, and removes the occasion for more cruelty.
stoic_reason: His act proceeds from a correct judgement: the goblet is a mere external and the slave's life is a preferred thing worth protecting. As emperor, and as a guest who sees a wrong done in front of him, his role calls on him to stop it (R1, R6; Discourses 2.10). 'Shocked' alone does not show an assented passion such as anger; it reads most naturally as a first movement or a rational recoil from cruelty (R2, R3, R4).

source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader
source_quote: Philip bade them be silent, and let this Thersites depart safe and sound. ... he allowed a man to curse him with impunity.
source_reason: "But do you," said he, "you other ambassadors, tell the Athenians that those who say such things are much more arrogant than those who hear them without revenging themselves."
source_lesson: Let everyone, then, say to himself, whenever he is provoked, "Am I more powerful than Philip? yet he allowed a man to curse him with impunity.
source_verdict: it was an especial virtue of Philip's to endure insults patiently, and was a great safeguard of his kingdom.
stoic_judgement: He treats the insult as no harm to himself and revenge as no good. He also holds that sparing the ambassador is what his role as king requires. The scene shows this when he bids the indignant bystanders be silent, lets the man 'depart safe', and says that 'those who say such things are more arrogant than those who hear them unrevenged'.
stoic_reason: By Handbook 20 it is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your judgement, and this king does not assent to the impression of injury. He checks the anger around him and keeps faith with an envoy as his role asks (R1, R2 by contrast, R6). His closing remark reads most naturally as a reasoned judgement about where the fault lies. Read as a bid for reputation, it would concern an external, which is a smaller possibility.

other: You see the worst-tempered orator, dining in his own chamber with a client who agrees to whatever he says, unable to bear it, exclaim, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!"
self: You, the worst-tempered orator, dining in your own chamber with a client who agrees to whatever you say, cannot bear it and exclaim, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us!"
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Anger 3.8 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, advising the reader
source_quote: Caelius could not bear his obsequious agreement, and exclaimed, "Do contradict me in something, that there may be two of us\!" Yet even he, who was angry at not being angry, soon recovered his temper, because he had no one to fight with.
source_reason: The other thought it best to agree to whatever he said, and to play second fiddle
source_lesson: If, then, we are conscious of an irascible disposition, let us especially choose for our friends those who will look and speak as we do: they will pamper us and lead us into a bad habit of listening to nothing that does not please us, but it will be good to give our anger respite and repose.
source_verdict: If, then, we are conscious of an irascible disposition, let us especially choose for our friends those who will look and speak as we do: they will pamper us and lead us into a bad habit of listening to nothing that does not please us, but it will be good to give our anger respite and repose.
stoic_judgement: He treats the client's constant agreement, which is not up to him, as intolerable, as though he needs someone to strive against. The vignette shows this in "the worst-tempered orator", "unable to bear it" and "exclaim". A less likely reading is that he is rejecting flattery and wants honest counsel ("that there may be two of us").
stoic_reason: Being unable to bear another's conduct is a disturbance from his judgement about an external thing, not from the thing itself (Handbook 5, 20). As an assented passion shown in an outburst, it is acting badly (R2). The reading that he rightly refuses a flatterer is possible but less likely given "worst-tempered" and "unable to bear it" (R1).

other: You see a conqueror willingly accept a city's citizenship from its envoys, thinking not of who offered it but that he was made equal to Hercules, the only stranger they had enrolled before.
self: You willingly accept a city's citizenship from its envoys, thinking not of who offered it but that you are made equal to Hercules, the only stranger they had enrolled before.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 1.13 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise On Benefits, addressing Liberalis
source_quote: Alexander willingly accepted the proffered honour, invited the ambassadors to his table, and showed them other courtesies.
source_reason: He did not think of who offered the citizenship, but to whom they had granted it; and being altogether the slave of glory ... fancied that the heaven to which his vanity aspired was indeed opening before him when he was made equal to Hercules.
source_verdict: In what indeed did that frantic youth, whose only merit was his lucky audacity, resemble Hercules? Hercules conquered nothing for himself; he travelled throughout the world, not coveting for himself but liberating the countries which he conquered, an enemy to bad men, a defender of the good, a peacemaker both by sea and land; whereas the other was from his boyhood a brigand and desolator of nations, a pest to his friends and enemies alike, whose greatest joy was to be the terror of all mankind, forgetting that men fear not only the fiercest but also the most cowardly animals, because of their evil and venomous nature.
source_missing: Alexander's conquests were self-serving plunder that had already flattered him into believing he was more than man, which is why accepting equality with Hercules, who conquered only to liberate, was vanity.
stoic_judgement: He treats the glory of being ranked with Hercules, a matter of reputation and so not up to him, as a good worth having. The vignette shows this: he accepts 'willingly', 'thinking not of who offered it but that he was made equal to Hercules'.
stoic_reason: Accepting a citizenship is an intermediate act, neither good nor bad in itself. By R1 the verdict follows the judgement behind it, and here that judgement is a craving for reputation, which Handbook 1 places among things 'not under our control'. By R2 and Handbook 19 an assented desire for such externals is acting badly: one who wants to be ranked with heroes rather than to be free has placed his good outside his moral purpose.

self: You are a slave, and you draw the ring bearing the emperor's portrait from your drunken master's finger as he takes up a chamber-pot, then show it on your own finger when an informer accuses your master.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.26 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: drew the ring from the finger of his drunken master... the slave showed the ring upon his own finger
source_lesson: After so many instances, can we doubt that a master may sometimes receive a benefit from a slave?

stoic_judgement: The slave most likely judges that he should keep faith with his master and shield him from a ruinous charge, even at some risk to himself. He acts before the image is defiled: he "draw[s] the ring bearing the emperor's portrait from his drunken master's finger as the master takes up a chamber-pot." When "an informer accuses his master," he openly shows the ring "on his own finger," which answers the charge with the plain fact.
stoic_reason: Read from the act, his role and the setting (R1, R6), this is a slave doing what his relation to his master asks: guarding him, faithfully and with foresight, from an accusation that is not up to the master to prevent. He uses no deceit, only shows what is true, and steps into the informer's attention. That is an appropriate act done from a correct judgement, so it is acting well for a person making progress (R5).

self: You, an emperor asked by a praetorian guardsman for help to pay his debts, order the money paid and add offensive reproaches, not wishing more friends to come with the same request.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 2.7 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to Liberalis
source_quote: When Marius Nepos of the praetorian guard asked Tiberius Caesar for help to pay his debts, Tiberius asked him for a list of his creditors; this is calling a meeting of creditors, not paying debts. When the list was made out, Tiberius wrote to Nepos telling him that he had ordered the money to be paid, and adding some offensive reproaches.
source_reason: Tiberius, however, had some design in doing so; I imagine he did not wish more of his friends to come to him with the same request.
source_lesson: His mode of proceeding was, perhaps, successful in restraining men’s extravagant desires by shame, but he who wishes to confer benefits must follow quite a different path.
source_verdict: In all ways you should make your benefit as acceptable as possible by presenting it in the most attractive form; but the method of Tiberius is not to confer benefits, but to reproach. ... This is not an act of generosity, but a reprimand.
stoic_judgement: He treats sparing himself, or the treasury, from further requests as a good worth getting by humiliating the man he helps. The vignette shows this in 'add offensive reproaches, not wishing more friends to come with the same request': the insult is a deliberate tool of deterrence, not a correction aimed at the guardsman's good.
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R6, the act follows from its judgement. Paying the debt is a preferred, fitting act for a ruler toward a man in his service, but adding offensive reproaches to keep others away uses a man's dignity as a means to protect externals (money, freedom from petitions). That is contrary to the kindness and good fellowship his role asks of him. The generosity is real, so some weight goes to 'well', but the act as a whole proceeds most likely from a bad judgement.
also_in: Seneca, On Benefits (c. 56-64 CE; Miriam Griffin and Brad Inwood, 2011)

self: You, a slave physician ordered by your besieged master to give him poison, give a harmless drug and ask the master's son to keep you in custody till the result shows whether it was poison.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.24 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca
source_quote: Then the slave assented, and gave him a harmless drug to drink. When Domitius fell asleep after drinking this, the slave went to his son, and said, “Give orders for my being kept in custody until you learn from the result whether I have given your father poison or no.”
source_lesson: After so many instances, can we doubt that a master may sometimes receive a benefit from a slave? Why need the person of the giver detract from the thing which he gives?
source_verdict: Domitius lived, and Caesar saved his life; but his slave had saved it before.
stoic_judgement: He treats keeping his master alive as more fitting than obeying an order to kill him, and treats his good faith as something to keep in the open. He does not try to shield himself. The words that show this: 'give a harmless drug' instead of the ordered poison, and 'ask the master's son to keep him in custody till the result shows whether it was poison'. Offering himself for custody suggests he puts fidelity and being seen to deal honestly above his own safety, which is not up to him.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R6, the act reads as coming from a correct judgement in his role as physician and household member. He holds to what is by nature preferred (his master's life, Discourses 2.10). He gives up control over his own safety by submitting to custody, which shows good faith rather than deceit for profit (Handbook 52). The substitution deceives the master, which keeps a real share of probability on 'badly'.

self: You, a Lacedaemonian amid courtiers flattering the Persian king, alone tell him his unwieldy multitude is a danger to its chief, because an army too large cannot be governed, and cannot long exist.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 6.31 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing the reader who wants to repay a prosperous benefactor
source_quote: Demaratus, the Lacedaemonian, alone told him that the disorganized and unwieldy multitude in which he trusted, was in itself a danger to its chief
source_reason: because it possessed only weight without strength; for an army which is too large cannot be governed, and one which cannot be governed, cannot long exist.
source_lesson: He deserved his reward before he asked for it, but how wretched must the nation have been, in which there was no one who would speak the truth to the king except one man who did not speak it to himself.
source_verdict: He deserved his reward before he asked for it
stoic_judgement: He treats telling the king the truth as what his role of adviser requires, and treats the king's favour, and the risk of displeasing him, as not up to him and not a good to buy with flattery. The scene shows this in 'amid courtiers flattering', 'alone tell him' and the stated reason, 'an army too large cannot be governed, and cannot long exist.'
stoic_reason: Read from the scene (R1), the most likely judgement is a correct one: like the singer who does not need applause (Discourses 2.13), he does not crave the king's approval. He gives the counsel his role calls for (R6), with a reason stated, so he acts well as a person making progress (R5). The choice to speak against fear of the king and the crowd's pressure is courage; frank, honest counsel to the one he serves is justice (R8).

self: You, receiving subscriptions from friends to cover your expenses in exhibiting public games, refuse a large sum sent by a man of bad character: "Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?"
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 2.21 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, addressing Liberalis
source_quote: when he was receiving subscriptions from many of his friends to cover his expenses in exhibiting public games, would not receive a large sum which was sent him by Fabius Persicus
source_reason: Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?
source_lesson: If you want an instance of magnanimity, take the case of Julius Graecinus, whom Caius Caesar put to death merely on the ground that he was a better man than it suited a tyrant for anyone to be.
source_verdict: If you want an instance of magnanimity, take the case of Julius Graecinus ... Ought we to call this receiving presents, or rather taking one's pick of the senate?
stoic_judgement: He treats the large sum, an external not up to him, as worth less than his own self-respect and consistency. Being put under obligation to a man of bad character is something he will not accept for money. The words show it: he 'refuse[s] a large sum sent by a man of bad character', asking 'Am I to accept a present from a man when I would not accept his offer to drink a glass of wine with him?'
stoic_reason: Money for the games is only material for the moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). His stated reason shows a correct judgement: he puts his own moral purpose above a preferred indifferent and keeps his dealings with others consistent, so by R1 and R5 the act is done well. A small share goes to the reading that he refuses for show or reputation, which would be vanity.

source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Tranquillity of Mind 5 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his letter to his friend Serenus
source_quote: Yet Socrates was in the midst of the city, and consoled its mourning Fathers, encouraged those who despaired of the republic, by his reproaches brought rich men, who feared that their wealth would be their ruin, to a tardy repentance of their avarice, and moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters.
source_lesson: you may know, therefore, that even in an oppressed state a wise man can find an opportunity for bringing himself to the front, and that in a prosperous and flourishing one wanton insolence, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices bear sway.
source_verdict: moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him, because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters.
modernised: [{"source": "its mourning Fathers", "vignette": "its mourning elders", "why": "'Fathers' is the Roman title for senators or leading citizens; a reader today would take it literally as parents grieving their children."}]
stoic_judgement: He treats the tyrants' power over bodies, property and lives as not an evil to be feared, and his duty as a philosopher and citizen (to console, encourage and correct his fellow citizens) as what is up to him. The scene suggests this in 'in a city where thirty tyrants have slain thirteen hundred citizens', where he still acts openly by 'consoling its mourning elders, encouraging those who despair of the republic, and reproaching rich men for their avarice'.
stoic_reason: He acts in his role (R6, Discourses 2.10) toward what is naturally to be preferred, the good of his city, and he does not let fear of what is not up to him (Handbook 1, 5) stop him. His consolation is sympathy in words for the bereaved (Handbook 16, R4), and he turns others from craving externals. The most likely reading is that his act proceeds from correct judgements (R1, Discourses 4.8).

self: You, an exile told that civil war will soon restore all exiles, answer, "My wish is that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than mourn at my having returned."
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 6.37 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his treatise to Liberalis, citing Hecaton for the story of Callistratus
source_quote: did not wish to be restored to their homes at the cost of a public disaster, but preferred that two should suffer unjustly than that all should suffer alike
source_reason: My wish is, that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than that she should mourn at my having returned.
source_lesson: These two persons, who did not wish to be restored to their homes at the cost of a public disaster, but preferred that two should suffer unjustly than that all should suffer alike, are thought to have acted like good citizens; and in like manner it does not accord with the character of a grateful man, to wish that his benefactor may fall into troubles which he may dispel; because, even though he may mean well to him, yet he wishes him evil.
source_verdict: are thought to have acted like good citizens
stoic_judgement: He treats his own return from exile, an external not up to him, as worth less than his country being spared a civil war. He also prefers that the injustice of his banishment stand openly, so the country 'should blush', rather than be undone at the country's cost, so it should 'mourn at my having returned'. The words 'My wish is that my country should blush at my being banished, rather than mourn at my having returned' show this.
stoic_reason: He does not crave the external (return, office, standing) and so is not 'tossed to and fro' by those who could procure it (Discourses 1.4, Handbook 1). As a citizen he puts what is due to his country above a preferred indifferent, which is acting well from a correct judgement (R1, R6). His 'wish' reads as rational wishing, not craving (R4, DL 7.116). A minor alternative reading is that he cares about the country's shame, which is its reputation and not up to him.
also_in: Seneca, On Benefits (c. 56-64 CE; Miriam Griffin and Brad Inwood, 2011)

self: You laughingly refuse the emperor's offer of two hundred thousand sesterces, saying that if the emperor meant to tempt you, he ought to have offered his entire kingdom.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 7.11 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, the author, recounting what he says he has heard about Demetrius
source_quote: he laughingly refused it, thinking it unworthy of himself to boast of having refused so small a sum
source_reason: If he meant to tempt me, he ought to have tried to do so by offering his entire kingdom.
source_lesson: I must here repeat a proof of his magnanimity.
source_verdict: I must here repeat a proof of his magnanimity.
stoic_judgement: He treats the money as no good worth his freedom or his moral purpose, and the emperor's offer as an attempt to buy him. The words 'if the emperor meant to tempt him' show he reads the gift as a lure, and 'laughingly refuse' shows the sum does not move him.
stoic_reason: The act proceeds from the correct judgement that wealth is not up to us and is only material for the moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). It is the judgement of one who wishes 'not to be a praetor... but a free man' (Handbook 19), so it is acting well while making progress (R1, R5). He refuses as a philosopher whose role is not to be bought (R6). Some weight goes to 'badly' because the jibe could come from vanity rather than indifference, though the scene does not show this.
