source_lesson: I shall therefore ask for the return of a benefit, whenever I am either reduced to great straits, or where by doing so I shall act to the advantage of him from whom I ask it.
source_verdict: To act as he did is not so much to ask for a return as to take it when it lies in a convenient position ready for us, although we have to stretch out our hands in order to receive it.
stoic_judgement: He most likely treats winning his lawsuit, an external not up to him, as a good worth securing through Caesar's personal debt to him. The scene suggests this with "whose cause against his neighbours is going against him" and the timing of his reminder. The stated reason, "his commander's memory was confused by a multitude of incidents", allows a milder reading: he is only correcting a lapse so that his old service is known.
stoic_reason: Pursuing one's property is pursuing a preferred indifferent and can be appropriate (Discourses 2.10). But pressing a benefactor's claim to turn a losing case reads as craving an outcome outside his control and subordinating himself to the one who can procure it (Discourses 1.4, 2.13; R1, R2). The scene does not make clear which judgement moves him, so no reading is clearly most likely (R1, R9).

self: You and another slave drive your mistress through the captured city, telling the victors she is a most cruel mistress you are leading away for punishment, so she might be saved from murder.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle it: Epictetus holds that one ought not to lie (Handbook 52), but he gives no rule on deceiving would-be murderers to save an innocent life. This deceit is not for profit and is aimed at killers. His framing makes the protective judgement fitting, but it does not settle whether the lie used as the means is acting badly.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Benefits 3.23 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, citing Claudius Quadrigarius
source_quote: they ran before every one else along the streets, which they well knew, to the house in which they had been slaves, and drove their mistress before them; when they were asked who she might be, they answered that she was their mistress, and a most cruel one, and that they were leading her away for punishment. They led her outside the walls, and concealed her with the greatest care until the fighting was over; ... they also returned to their own countrymen, and themselves restored their mistress to them.
source_reason: if thereby their mistress might be saved from murder
source_lesson: Believe me, it is the mark of no slavish soul to purchase a noble deed by the semblance of crime.
source_verdict: Believe me, it is the mark of no slavish soul to purchase a noble deed by the semblance of crime.
stoic_judgement: The slaves treat their mistress's life as worth protecting at risk to themselves, and treat deceiving the victors as the fitting means. The vignette shows this in 'so she might be saved from murder' and in their pretending she is 'a most cruel mistress they are leading away for punishment'. The most likely reading is loyalty and kindness acted on with reason, not a craving for any external of their own.
stoic_reason: By R1 and R6, the act comes from the judgement that, as members of her household, they should protect her life. That life is a preferred indifferent that one should 'cleave to' (Discourses 2.10), and protecting it is kindness, which falls under justice. Facing armed victors with the ruse is endurance of danger. The means is a lie, though, and Epictetus names 'one ought not to lie' as a first principle (Handbook 52). So a reading on which the deceit is a fault keeps some weight.

source_lesson: There is no disgrace in altering one’s plans according to circumstances.
source_verdict: There is no inconsistency in giving up an intention which we have discovered to be wrong and have condemned as wrong; we ought candidly to admit, “I thought that it was something different; I have been deceived.”

stoic_judgement: The king treats doing right by the rescuer, and keeping hospitality's claims, as what matters. He does not treat his own earlier grant or his pride as something to defend. The words that show this: on reading the sharp letter he orders "the property restored", undoing his own gift, and gives the stated purpose of the branding: "so men may see how sacred is the table of hospitality."
stoic_reason: In his role as king and judge (R6), he corrects his own unjust grant once he is shown it, and he punishes the soldier's betrayal of his host for a stated public reason, not one of personal grievance. Read by the judgement behind the act (R1), this is most likely acting well. Some probability stays on anger at the rebuke or at the soldier driving the harsh branding (R2; Discourses 1.18).

source_lesson: How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease\!
source_verdict: How far happier is he who is indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive himself of with the greatest ease\!
stoic_judgement: He treats his own freedom from need as what matters, and the runaway slave, who is property and not up to him, as not worth pursuing. He also treats depending on externals as shameful. The scene shows this in two places: "does not think him worth fetching back" and "It is a shame that he should be able to live without me, and I not without him."
stoic_reason: Per Discourses 1.4 and Handbook 1, one who craves what is not under his control must subordinate himself to those who can procure or prevent it. This man refuses to make his contentment hang on an external and acts from that correct judgement, so the act is well done (R1, R5). Property is a preferred indifferent, but declining to pursue it here comes from a sound judgement about what is up to him, not from neglect of a duty his role plainly requires (R6).

Nothing in the scene shows the judgement that the death is an evil (Handbook 5, 16), so the most likely reading is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5). source_reason: you are enquiring whether our souls are immortal, but I shall presently know... "I have decided," answered Kanus, "at that most swiftly-passing moment of all to watch whether the spirit will be conscious of the act of leaving the body."
source_lesson: Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further.
source_verdict: Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer... it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was... Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life
stoic_judgement: He treats his coming death as nothing to dread, since it is not up to him. He treats the honest record of the game as what still matters, because that is up to him and his companion. The words that show it: summoned 'to join those going to be executed', he calmly 'count[s] his men' and warns, 'Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won.'
stoic_reason: His steady counting and his concern for truth at the moment of execution read as the correct judgement that death is not an evil (Handbook 5) and that only his own use of impressions and honesty are his own (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.29). An act that proceeds from correct judgements is well done (Discourses 4.8, R1, R5). There is a small chance the jest is bravado for others' applause (Discourses 2.13), but the scene gives no hint of that.

On the other, Epictetus allows the open door when one's role (prosopon) can no longer be kept with honour (Discourses 1.2, 1.24-25), which would be an appropriate act done from a correct judgement (R1, R5, R6).

self: You, a Roman general, embrace your dying younger brother and receive his last kiss, then restrain your grief and make the heart-broken army, claiming the corpse, grieve only as it becomes Romans to grieve.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Polybius 15 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, imagining the Emperor Caesar himself addressing Polybius in consolation (the exempla are put in Caesar's own voice: 'my paternal uncle', 'my father')
source_quote: he embraced him and received his last kiss, but he nevertheless restrained not only his own grief but that of others, and when the whole army, not merely sorrowful but heart-broken, claimed the corpse of their Drusus for themselves, he made them grieve only as it became Romans to grieve, and taught them that they must observe military discipline not only in fighting but also in mourning.
source_lesson: It is your duty to imitate their constancy in enduring and triumphing over suffering, as far as it is permitted to a mere man to follow in the footsteps of the immortals.
source_verdict: He could not have checked the tears of others had he not first repressed his own.
stoic_judgement: He treats his brother's death as something he must not judge an evil to be overwhelmed by, and treats both his affection and his role as commander as calling for composed, fitting conduct. The words that suggest this: he embraces the dying brother and receives his last kiss (affection), then 'restrain[s] his grief' and makes the army grieve 'only as it became Romans to grieve' (keeping in mind what a general owes his men).
stoic_reason: Affection that is also reasonable is 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11; R4). Restraining grief is refusing assent to the judgement that the loss is an evil (Handbook 5, 16; R2, R4). Remembering that he is a general and acting as the role asks toward a grieving army is appropriate (Discourses 2.10; R6). Read as a whole, the scene shows acting well as one making progress (R1, R5).

source_quote: you restored to the use of man that genius of your father for which he had suffered, and made him in real truth immortal by publishing as an eternal memorial of him those books which that bravest of men had written with his own blood

source_verdict: You have done a great service to Roman literature: a large part of Cordus's books had been burned; a great service to posterity, who will receive a true account of events, which cost its author so dear; and a great service to himself, whose memory flourishes and ever will flourish... stoic_judgement: She most likely judges that what is owed to her father and to her country is to preserve and make known his true account. She treats honouring a parent and keeping the truth as her part, and waits for a time when this can be done. The vignette shows this in 'publishing what survives of her father's true account' and 'when times change'.
stoic_reason: As a daughter, her role (Handbook 30; Discourses 2.10) calls for honouring her father, and DL 7.108 names honouring parents and country among befitting acts. Read from the scene (R1), the act most likely proceeds from a correct judgement about what is due, not from craving reputation as a good, so it counts as acting well while making progress (R5, R6).

He gives no assent to grief at a loss outside his control (R2, Handbook 5), so the most likely reading is acting well as one making progress (R1, R5). Feigning not to hear is aimed at not interrupting the rite, not at deceit for gain, so Handbook 52 does not tell against him.

source_quote: Annoyed with him, I seized on the nearest excuse to vent my anger.
source_reason: This wouldn't be happening if they were kept fertilized and watered.
source_lesson: My suburban villa has done me a service; it has brought my age before me at every turn. Let us embrace old age and love it.

stoic_judgement: He treats the state of his trees, and his manager's supposed neglect, as an evil done to him that deserves anger. The vignette shows this in "annoyed with his property manager", "seize on the nearest excuse to vent his anger", and the accusation "This wouldn't be happening if they were kept fertilized and watered."
stoic_reason: This is an assented passion, not a first movement (R2, not R3). He has already let himself be carried away by the judgement that an external thing, his trees and another man's conduct, is bad and that he is wronged (Handbook 5, 20). He then acts on that anger by blaming his manager on a pretext, which is acting badly (R1, R2).

self: When a tyrant threatens you with death and even with want of burial, you answer, “My half pint of blood is in your power: what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it.”
source: Seneca, Complete Works: On Tranquillity of Mind 14 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, writing to his friend Serenus
source_quote: A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. “You are able to please yourself,” he answered, “my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it.”
source_lesson: The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works ; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself ; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes.
source_verdict: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life
stoic_judgement: He treats his body, his life and what happens to his corpse as not up to him and not evils. Only his own judgement matters to him. The words that show it: "My half pint of blood is in your power" and "I care [not] whether I rot above ground or under it."
stoic_reason: He sorts things correctly into what is up to us and what is not (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.1). He refuses to treat death or lack of burial as dreadful: the judgement 'death is dreadful' is the dreadful thing (Handbook 5). So he acts from a correct judgement and does not assent to fear (R1, R2, R5). The scene shows no passion, though calling the tyrant 'a fool' leaves a small chance the retort comes from pride rather than calm.

In the other, he punishes himself for failing at an external, the king's death, which suggests he judged that failure an evil. speaker: Seneca, replying to Lucilius's question why, if the world is ruled by providence, so many evils befall good men
source_quote: he grasped the enemy’s fire with his right hand, and of his own accord paid the penalty of his mistake? because he overcame the King with his hand when it was burned, though he could not when it held a sword
source_lesson: it is ill fortune alone that discovers these glorious examples.
source_verdict: Was Mucius unhappy, because he grasped the enemy’s fire with his right hand, and of his own accord paid the penalty of his mistake? because he overcame the King with his hand when it was burned, though he could not when it held a sword? Would he have been happier, if he had warmed his hand in his mistress’s bosom;
stoic_judgement: He seems to treat his failure as a fault of his own that he must answer for, and the pain and loss of his hand as nothing to fear. The words that show this: "could not overcome the enemy King when his hand held a sword", "grasp the enemy's fire with his right hand", "of his own accord paying the penalty of his mistake".
stoic_reason: Grasping the fire of his own accord shows a judgement that the body and pain are not evils, which is endurance and so courage (R1, R8; Handbook 1). But if the 'penalty' is self-punishment for an outcome that was not up to him, it suggests he judged that external failure an evil, which would be a passion (R2; Discourses 2.13). Burning his hand also throws away a preferred indifferent, and the scene gives no reason his role required it (R6; Discourses 2.10). Neither reading is clearly more likely.

other: You see the emperor's sister, who has lost her son, the emperor's chosen heir, raging against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child seems now transferred to the wife's son.
self: You, the emperor's sister, having lost your son, the emperor's chosen heir, rage against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for your own child seems now transferred to her son.
source: Seneca, Complete Works: Consolation to Marcia 2 (tr. Aubrey Stewart)
speaker: Seneca, in his letter of consolation to Marcia, who has mourned her son for three years
source_quote: His mother never ceased to weep and sob during her whole life, never endured to listen to wholesome advice, never even allowed her thoughts to be diverted from her sorrow. She remained during her whole life just as she was during the funeral, with all the strength of her mind intently fixed upon one subject. I do not say that she lacked the courage to shake off her grief, but she refused to be comforted, thought that it would be a second bereavement to lose her tears, and would not have any portrait of her darling son, nor allow any allusion to be made to him. She hated all mothers, and raged against Livia with especial fury, because it seemed as though the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child was now transferred to Livia’s son. Passing all her days in darkened rooms and alone, not conversing even with her brother, she refused to accept the poems which were composed in memory of Marcellus, and all the other honours paid him by literature, and closed her ears against all consolation. She lived buried and hidden from view, neglecting her accustomed duties, and actually angry with the excessive splendour of her brother’s prosperity, in which she shared. Though surrounded by her children and grandchildren, she would not lay aside her mourning garb, though by retaining it she seemed to put a slight upon all her relations, in thinking herself bereaved in spite of their being alive.
source_reason: because it seemed as though the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child was now transferred to Livia’s son.
source_lesson: Plague on it\! what madness this is, to punish one’s self because one is unfortunate, and not to lessen, but to increase one’s ills!
source_verdict: I here put the best construction on what is really most contemptible and foreign to your character. ... If, on the other hand, showing a milder and better regulated spirit, you try to follow the example of the latter most exalted lady, you will not be in misery, nor will you wear your life out with suffering.
source_missing: That her grief and rage lasted her whole life: she refused all consolation and advice, shut herself away in darkness, and hated all mothers, never letting the sorrow pass.
stoic_judgement: She treats the brilliant prospect (succession, office, rank) that was in store for her son as a great good, its passing to the wife's son as an evil done to her, and the wife as the one who wrongs her. The vignette shows this in "raging against the emperor's wife, because the brilliant prospect once in store for her own child seems now transferred to the wife's son."
stoic_reason: Office and reputation are not under our control (Handbook 1), so raging and envy over another's son receiving them is an assented passion, the judgement that an external is good or evil (R2; Handbook 19, 20; Discourses 1.18). "Raging" against a person, with a stated reason, is sustained assent rather than a first movement (R3, R7), and grief judged an evil is the fault, not the tears (R4).

'Cheerfully and willingly drain the poison', 'as though it were a charm to make him immortal' and 'arguing about death until death itself' show he has not assented to the impression that death is an evil, and keeps using his reason to the end.
stoic_reason: The act comes from the correct judgement that death, which is not up to him, is not an evil (Handbook 5; R1). He shows no assented fear (R2), and his willing, cheerful acceptance is rational joy, not a passion (R4). So he is acting well as a person whose judgement is sound (R5).

source: Seneca, Letters on Ethics to Lucilius: Letter 27.5–8 (2015, tr. Margaret Graver & A. A. Long)
speaker: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, giving instructions to himself while Lucilius stands by
source_quote: So he devised an expedient: he spent a great deal of money on slaves, one of whom was to know Homer by heart, another Hesiod, plus nine more, each assigned to one of the lyric poets. It is no wonder the cost was high, since any that were not to be found he paid to have instructed. Once he had assembled this staff, he began to pester his dinner guests. ... source_reason: he wanted to appear learned
source_lesson: Excellence of mind cannot be borrowed or bought. I think too that if it were for sale, it would not find a buyer. Yet wickedness is purchased every day.
source_verdict: Excellence of mind cannot be borrowed or bought. I think too that if it were for sale, it would not find a buyer. Yet wickedness is purchased every day.
stoic_judgement: He treats seeming learned in others' eyes, a matter of reputation and not up to him, as a good worth great expense, rather than seeking learning in his own moral purpose. The vignette states the motive: "wanting to appear learned", "spend a great deal of money", and "whom he asks for verses to quote" (borrowed recitation for show, not his own study).
stoic_reason: Reputation is not under our control (Handbook 1). Craving it is the judgement that an external is a good, like the citharoede who wants applause (Discourses 2.13; Handbook 19). Acting from that judgement is acting badly (Discourses 4.8; R1, R2), and it is vanity, which falls in the field of temperance (R8).

stoic_judgement: He most likely treats a friend in serious illness as someone owed his presence and care, enough to set aside a day of his busy money-making. Shown by 'spend the whole day at a seriously ill friend's bedside' despite 'investing at home and abroad with money flooding in'. His wealth and his sudden death are things not up to him, and the scene states no judgement that he craves the money.
stoic_reason: Attending a sick friend is an appropriate act of one's role as a friend (R6; DL 7.108, 'intercourse with friends'), and the likeliest reading is that it comes from affection joined with reason, which is 'right and good' (Discourses 1.11; R1, R4). His wealth and his death by angina are externals, materials and not acts, so they do not by themselves make him act badly (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.29). Some weight goes to a motive the scene does not show, such as duty done only for show, or a mind still fixed on gain.

Piety offered as a trade for things not up to us shows that he places good in externals, not in his own moral purpose (Discourses 1.29). It is the citharoede wanting applause (Discourses 2.13): piety kept up for a return is not right opinion about the gods. Prayer alone would not be a fault, and the request might be for others or might be modest, so some weight goes to the other readings.

stoic_judgement: He treats what fortune held for him as never truly his, and what he did himself, his giving, as the only thing that stays his own. stoic_reason: Read most likely as a correct judgement that externals (fortune, power, even life) are not up to us and that only his own acts of moral purpose remain his (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.29). source_lesson: Yet these people have not conferred a benefit on the defendant, although they helped him, because what is in question is where the weapon was aimed and not where it struck, and what distinguishes a benefit from an injury is not the outcome but the intention.

source_missing: The undue influence came from people who were trying to get the defendant condemned. They meant to harm him, and their pressure backfired.
stoic_judgement: The judges were "prepared to condemn a man for a crime," so on the merits they seem to have judged him guilty. They then "refuse to condemn him on account of undue influence." The most likely reading is that their verdict turned on something outside the case, the influence brought to bear on them, and not on the man's guilt. If they were swayed, they treated what powerful people want, or the gains and losses that come with it, as good or evil. If they acquitted to avoid looking pressured, they treated their reputation for independence as a good, above giving the man what was due. A less likely reading is that they rightly refused because the influence had corrupted the case against him.
stoic_reason: In their role as judges (R6), duty asks them to apportion what is due by the merits of the case. Letting an external, such as pressure or reputation, decide a verdict they had already reached is an act from a bad judgement about what is up to them (R1, Discourses 4.8). The other reading, refusing to let a corrupted prosecution stand, would be acting well. The scene makes this less likely, but cannot rule it out.

source_lesson: on the one hand, Cicero displayed political savvy and an ability to compromise in order to achieve his objectives, though at times his willingness to adjust to the situation on the ground bordered on hypocrisy or opportunism. On the other hand, Cato was the light of virtue and integrity that inspired his followers, and that was much admired by Cicero, even though it was that very same sense of honor that led him to fail to build the sort of political coalition that might have turned the fortunes of the Republic and avoided descent into empire.

The words that suggest it: 'pushed a law raising the penalty for bribery', 'offer to defend the patently guilty consul-elect', 'because he needs two new consuls to hold firm against a conspirator'.

The safety of the country is a preferred indifferent he should act for (Discourses 2.10), but a guilty man escaping what is due is an injustice. Using the court to secure an external outcome is most plausibly a judgement that the outcome outweighs justice, which is acting badly. Still, the consul's duty to his country gives a reasonable defence for the act (DL 7.107), so 'well' keeps real weight.

stoic_reason: The body is not under our control, and it is not the pain but the judgement that it is dreadful that disturbs (Handbook 1, 5). He corrects that impression in his own mind and endures, which is acting well as one making progress (R1, R2 by contrast, R5), and the field is enduring pain (R8).

source_lesson: Cultivation is called for in cases like the one Seneca describes above, as when learning how to take satisfaction from simple and natural pleasures.

His reaction is to a lack in externals ("his baker is out of bread"). He answers people offering to help ("the overseer, or the steward, or his tenants offer him some") with a dismissive exclamation, "Bad bread!"
stoic_reason: Food is an external, not up to him (Handbook 1). Complaining about the quality of what is freely offered reads as an assented aversion: he judges plain bread an evil and his preferred bread a good (R1, R2). Handbook 45 warns against blaming eating as such, but here the scene shows the judgement in his words, not just a habit. It also shows ungraciousness toward those who serve him, which falls short of what his role asks (R6).

Here the scene states that judgement: pleasure is pursued as the good, an assent to desire for an external. That is acting badly in the field of desire (R1, R2; Discourses 3.2, 1.29). The fault concerns appetite, so temperance is the virtue at stake (R8).

source_quote: weeping over the death of an eel-like fish that he owned; Crassus replied that the tears were more than Domitius had shed over his three late wives
source_lesson: Of the same nature are the irregular appetites of the mind; though they are often excited by trifles, they are equally disquieting with real wants: the Roman, who wept at the death of his lamprey, felt the same degree of sorrow that extorts tears on other occasions.

stoic_judgement: He most likely treats the death of a fish he owned, a piece of his property, as a real loss worth mourning: he is 'weeping over the death' of it. When mocked, he defends the tears and turns them into a jab at his mocker ('more than his mocker shed over his three late wives'). This suggests he holds to his grief and treats the ridicule as something to be repaid, not as nothing to him.
stoic_reason: A possession is 'not under our control' (Handbook 1). Weeping over it, and then standing by the weeping when challenged, reads as assent to the judgement that its loss is an evil, which is a passion of grief (R2, Handbook 5). Answering the ridicule with a counter-barb suggests he judged the mockery an injury needing reply (Handbook 20). The tears could in principle be an unwilled first movement (R3, R4), but defending them makes that less likely.

His words "How will he receive me, how will he listen to me?" show this. So does his pallor and trembling, which go with that spoken worry rather than with a sudden shock.

His spoken worry shows the paleness is more than a bare first movement (R3, fragment 9), though that reading keeps some probability.

Fragment 9 excuses only swift, unconsidered motions 'not from any anticipation of some evil' (R3), and this fear looks like anticipation of the emperor's power, so acting badly is the most likely reading.

The scientist withholds that blame and turns to his own faults, which is the mark of progress in Discourses 1.4 ("turned his attention to the question of his own moral purpose"). It also fits the view, in Discourses 1.18 and Handbook 42, that a wrongdoer is deceived and is no ground for contempt or anger; per R1 and R5 this is acting well.

source_verdict: Why do we fool ourselves? Our evil is not on the outside, it is within us, it is seated in our vitals – and it is that much harder to attain health when we do not know we are sick.
source_missing: That the man really is ambitious, extravagant and irritable, and is blaming Rome and his youth to avoid admitting vices that are his own. The vignette gives only his words, not that they are false, self-serving excuses.
stoic_judgement: He treats his ambition, spending and irritability as caused by things outside his choice (the city, his youth) rather than by his own judgements. He also implicitly treats the standing and display Rome 'requires' as things he must have. The words that show this: "there's no other way to live in Rome", "the city requires a significant outlay", "it's not my fault I'm irritable, that's just my youth."
stoic_reason: Choice, desire and aversion are up to us. Epictetus ascribes wrong action to 'no other cause than the decision of our will' (Discourses 1.11, Handbook 1), so blaming Rome and his youth is itself a false judgement about what is up to him. It is assent to the passions of ambition, craving and anger rather than resistance to them (R1, R2).

stoic_judgement: He treats the other man's act as a harm done to him, and harming him back as something still owed or still to come. The words "has already injured me" show he judges the other's deed an injury to himself. The "not yet" in "but I have not yet injured him" suggests he intends to pay it back.
stoic_reason: Under R1 and R2, the act follows his judgement. He judges that another person's deed, which is not up to him, has harmed him, and that returning the harm is fitting. For Epictetus it is your own judgement that you have been insulted (Handbook 20), and the wrongdoer harms only his own moral purpose (Discourses 1.18). So assenting to injury and planning retaliation is acting badly.

stoic_reason: The paleness is a first movement that comes before reason, which even the wise man cannot help (fragment 9). Without assent it is not the passion of fear, so it is neither well nor badly done (R3, R7). Refusing assent could be read as acting well in the field of assent, but the scene centres on the involuntary reaction (R1).

source_quote: For the latter, every time he went out into public, used to weep; the former used to laugh.

source_lesson: Things should be made light of, and taken more easily: it is more civilized to laugh at life than to bewail it.
source_verdict: we should imitate Democritus rather than Heraclitus. ... Things should be made light of, and taken more easily: it is more civilized to laugh at life than to bewail it.
stoic_judgement: He judges that everything people do is absurd, and he laughs at it each time he is in public. The words 'every time he goes out into public, laughs' and 'sees everything we do as absurdity' show a standing, wholesale verdict on all human acts, not a one-off reaction.
stoic_reason: Calling every act absurd passes sentence on others' acts without learning the judgement each one comes from. Epictetus forbids this in *Discourses* 4.8 and *Handbook* 45, and it is rash assent, the third field of *Discourses* 3.2 (R1). Laughter that is constant and public also goes against his instruction that laughter not be frequent or unrestrained (*Handbook* 33). A milder reading is possible: an undisturbed man who simply sees that people chase externals. It is less likely, because his verdict covers 'everything we do', good acts included.

stoic_reason: It is not the man who reviles you that insults you, but your judgement that he does (Handbook 20). Birth is 'not our own doing' (Handbook 1). He refuses to assent to the impression that a barbarian mother is a shame, and answers with good humour rather than a passion (R1, R2 in reverse). A small chance remains that the retort comes from wanting to win the exchange and protect his reputation, which is not up to him.

By craving what others can give or withhold, he subordinates himself to them (Discourses 1.4), so this is acting badly (R1, R2; not R3).

stoic_judgement: The judge treats the community's safety and deterring future harm as what his office requires. He treats his own anger as no part of the sentence. The vignette shows this in 'quietly', 'with no gnashing of the teeth' and 'for deterrence and the good of the community'. He also judges that the wives and children may be destroyed with the households ('along with wives and children') as a means to that end.

The words that show this are "calm and unmoved", "as examples", and "not so much that they may be destroyed as that their destruction may deter others".

Some doubt remains, because he aims at deterring others rather than the offender's own good, as fragment 22's 'curator and guardian' does.

What is up to us (Handbook 1) cannot be besieged, so dying rather than handing themselves over reads most likely as acting from a correct judgement (R1), enduring the fear of death (R8 courage). His guarded but friendly avoidance is caution and goodwill, which are good feelings and not passions (R4, DL 7.116). This is acting well as one making progress (R5).

The vignette shows this in 'always goes out and comes home with the same look' and 'a mind smooth and cheerful on all occasions, far remote from grief and above all from fear'.
stoic_reason: Grief and fear are judgements that externals are evils (Handbook 5, 19; Discourses 2.13). A mind that stays steady and cheerful while public calamity, which is outside his control, goes on shows correct judgements rather than assented passions (R1, R2, R4). Cheerfulness of this kind is a good feeling, not a fault (DL 7.116). Nothing in the scene suggests he neglects his role as a citizen (R6).

His pleasant remembrance is affection with reason, a rational joy rather than a passion, and so 'both affectionate and reasonable ... right and good' (R4, Discourses 1.11, DL 7.116). The act proceeds from correct judgements and is acting well while making progress (R1, R5).

chapter: Your Happiness Does Not Depend on Where You Live
speaker: Musonius Rufus, consoling an exiled person who complains about his exile
source_quote: Have you, or anyone else, seen me cringe before anyone just because I am an exile? Have you seen me thinking that I am worse off now than before? I will bet that you have never seen me groaning or moaning because of my exile.
source_reason: Even if I have been deprived of my country, my ability to endure exile has not been taken .
source_lesson: If you are wise, you will not consider exile as dreadful, since others bear it easily.
source_verdict: A courageous person is as courageous in exile as at home.
source_missing: The exile (Musonius himself) still speaks his mind freely: he has not been robbed of free speech or of the freedom to say what he thinks.
stoic_judgement: He treats exile, the loss of his country (an external, not up to him), as no evil, and treats his own faculty of enduring it as what matters and as still his own. The vignette shows this: 'does not ... think himself worse off than before', 'because though deprived of his country, his ability to endure exile has not been taken'.
stoic_reason: The judgement behind his conduct is stated and correct. Country is among the things not under our control, and the use of impressions is under it (Handbook 1, Discourses 1.1). So no passion of grief or fear is assented to (R2), and his bearing proceeds from correct judgement, which makes it well done (Discourses 4.8; R1, R5).

stoic_judgement: Most likely the poet holds, and puts before his audience, the view that freedom depends on being allowed to speak one's mind, an external that others grant or take away. The vignette suggests this in 'exiles lose their personal freedom when their freedom of speech is taken away' and 'the condition of a slave not to be able to speak what one thinks'. It is also possible the poet only gives the line to a character and does not hold it himself.
stoic_reason: By Epictetus's doctrine, freedom lies in our own moral purpose, the use of impressions, which no exile or tyrant can take away. Speech permitted by others is not under our control (Handbook 1; Discourses 1.1, 1.29), so judging its loss to be slavery is a false judgement about good and evil. Writing a play is in itself an intermediate act, though, and the verdict turns on whether the poet assents to this judgement or only dramatizes it (R1, R6).
